title: HomeView Code Suggests Future Support for AI Chatbot Apps, Anti-Spoofing Protection
content:
Code discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests Apple is laying the groundwork for chatbot apps on its upcoming HomeView smart home hub, according to the code investigator known as pdfu.


The software HomeView uses to display apps from a connected iPhone or iPad is said to have gained a "Conversational Apps" category in the latest beta. The update also reportedly adds preparations for two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions, but pdfu notes that it is "still not fully wired up." 

suggested on Sunday that chatbot apps might follow based on an unused flag in HomeView's software.

Anti-Spoofing Protection

In a separate finding, pdfu also discovered that HomeView includes anti-spoofing protection. Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2. 

Apple is also said to be working on a lockout cooldown system, similar to what happens when you enter the wrong passcode on an iPhone. A first lockout can be cleared immediately, but a second lockout brings a one-hour wait, a third a four-hour wait, and a fourth (or any further) lockout an eight-hour wait.

pdfu adds that the lockout cooldown periods are still in development, so for now any lockout can be cleared immediately by authenticating with an iPhone. Apple hasn't described either feature in its press materials.

HomeView Launches Next Week

HomeView launches on November 13 for $299, in both desktop and wall-mounted versions. Here's what Apple has announced so far:

7-inch Liquid Retina display, in a tabletop model with a speaker base and a wall-mounted model.

Face recognition for up to six users, each with a personal Home Screen with apps and widgets.

Siri AI, with conversations that continue in the Siri app on other Apple devices.

Personal content from Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My, shown when the enrolled user is recognized and their iPhone or iPad is nearby and recently unlocked.

Faces including Photos, Flow, Snoopy, Home Modular, and Home Camera.

Apple Music, Podcasts, News, and Apple TV, plus compatible third-party audio and video apps.

Handoff from iPhone, and multiroom audio with HomePod, HomePod mini, and AirPlay speakers.

FaceTime with Center Stage, Messages by voice or keyboard, and Intercom.

Step-by-step recipes from the web with hands-free timers.

Smart home controls, including a Home Camera face that shows up to nine live camera feeds.

With a supported iCloud+ subscription, recognition of people, pets, packages, and vehicles from compatible cameras.

Smoke and carbon monoxide alarm sound detection.

Support for Apple Home Collection accessories, other "Works with Apple Home" accessories, and Matter.

HomeView won't have an App Store. However, as we reported last month, it shows CarPlay-style third-party audio and video apps from a connected iPhone or iPad. HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc.

title: These Finder tips will make you a Mac pro
content:
Macworld





The Finder in macOS is where you spend the most time when using your Mac. It is the most important tool for managing files and folders; it’s the basis for installing and launching apps; it’s where you can manage iPhones and iPads; and a lot more. It’s the foundation for the macOS interface and for using your Mac hardware.
Many Mac users have been using the Finder every day for decades, often without making full use of its capabilities or customizing it to suit their own needs. You should make the most of your UI experience. Here are ten tips on how to get more out of the Finder.
Customize the toolbar
This is a very simple thing to do, but hardly anyone does. You should adjust the  Finder toolbar to suit your own needs. To do this, open a Finder window and right-click on the toolbar. You’ll see the Customize Toolbar option in the context menu. Select it, and a window will appear with additional functions and tools. You can click and drag icons to where you want them in the toolbar.
The AirDrop icon, for example, is useful if you transfer files often: once it’s been added to the Finder, you simply select an item and send it straight away. The buttons for burning blank discs, ejecting media, and accessing servers can also be useful, depending on your needs.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




You can also easily change the order of the icons. Simply click on one while holding down the Command key. To remove it from the toolbar, simply drag it out.
Quick Commands for photo editing and your own scripts
Quick Actions are small tools that you can access via the context menu (the menu that appears when you right-click an item). They allow you to quickly convert PNG to JPEG or create a PDF, for example.
Six system services are provided by default, though the options available in the context menu depend on the selected file type. For example, if you right-click on a video, you can access a function to trim the video. This is quicker and easier than using QuickTime Player.
For photos, you can quickly convert them to other formats such as JPEG; you can combine several PDFs into a single PDF file using Create PDF; rotate a photo; and remove the background from a photo (though this doesn’t always work). For image files and PDFs, there’s also the option to add annotations. This opens a window with the tools familiar from Preview, allowing you to add lines, red arrows, and other annotations.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




You can enable and disable these useful extensions under General > Login Items & Extensions > System Services. To do this, click on the ‘i’ icon there.
There’s even a way to add your own Quick Actions: to do this, simply select ‘Quick Action’ as the file type in Automator and create a workflow – such as resizing a photo to a specific width. Once created, the workflow is immediately available via the context menu.
Rename multiple files
You don’t need to resort to a tool like Renamer to rename dozens of files or folders. The Finder also has a built-in function for renaming files. However, it’s somewhat hidden.
To access the feature, select multiple files and choose Rename from the context menu. If you selected just a single file, you can only change the name within the Finder; the file will be selected for you automatically. However, if you’ve selected multiple files, a separate new window opens with several options.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Here you can choose from several renaming options; you can add text, replace text, or rename all files according to a new format. When replacing text, simply enter the original text and the new text in the two fields. When adding text, you can choose to add it at the beginning or the end, as a prefix or suffix.
The Format option is more complex, offering three choices: here you can choose between two numbering styles and adding the current date.
Manage the clipboards
Starting with macOS Tahoe, old clipboard contents can be saved by the system on request and are searchable via Spotlight. You’ll need to enable this feature first via the Spotlight system setting. You can also select a retention period; options are 8 hours, 30 minutes, and 7 days.
Once enabled, you can enter a search term into Spotlight to search the clipboard text. Alongside other results, you’ll then see a list of previous clipboard entries, marked with two small boxes. You can also press Command+4 or select Clipboard after opening Spotlight.
You can valso iew the current clipboard select Edit > Show Clipboard from the menu bar in Finder, and the current clipboard will be displayed in a simple window.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Hide all items on the Desktop
Apple now offers so many options for the Desktop and Dock that some people lose track of them all. For a long time, I overlooked the fact that the Desktop & Dock system setting can hide all items on the desktop completely.
To do this, go to the Desktop & Dock system settings and, under Show items, untick the box next to On the Desktop. You can later show all folders and files again using the same function.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




List invisible files and folders
The Mac actually has countless invisible folders and files on your system. Most are used by the system and are best left hidden, otherwise, your folders can quickly become cluttered. Sometimes, invisible files are left behind when you uninstall an app or delete a file.
All you need to do is press Command+Shift+. to see invisible files.  The first time you press the key combination, you see all hidden files and folders in the selected folder. Press it again, and they’ll disappear again.
Hide files or folders
You can make a file or folder invisible via Terminal: enter the command chflags hidden and add the path–drag and drop the file or folder into the Terminal window to do this.
Connect to a server
The Finder is also responsible for allowing you to connect via the network: to other Macs, the company server or even a Fritzbox with NAS functionality. Available servers are often listed automatically in the Finder under Network. You can connect manually via Go > Connect to Server. 
Even FTP is supported, but you can only download data. Uploads are not possible, and FTP servers using the SFTP or FTPS protocols are not supported. However, the FTP function is not always reliable and has often caused problems. It is not without reason that many experienced users prefer to use an FTP client such as Cyberduck for every FTP connection.
Make better use of Smart Folders
Smart Folders are very powerful, but unfortunately can be too fiddly. These ingenious folders are essentially saved search queries that update dynamically. You can save these folders once created and conveniently pin them to the sidebar. By default, however, the Finder links all search criteria using only simple AND conditions, as is familiar from Spotlight or the Google search engine.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




But the folder becomes truly smart with so-called Boolean operators. For example, when you’re looking for all image files but also all video files, or all files that are neither image files nor video files. (This might sound like a fiddly logic puzzle to you right now, but it can be very useful!)
Apple has hidden this option a little, presumably so as not to overwhelm beginners. First, create a smart folder as usual, for example, via File > New Smart Folder. Then click the + icon, and you can define the criteria for the items you want to appear in the folder. Click the + icon to add more definitions. Click the Save button to set the Smart Folder, and then when you open the folder, it will show all the items that fit the criteria you defined.

title: Got an iPhone Duo on Launch Day? Tomorrow Could Be Your Last Chance to Return It
content:
If you bought an iPhone Duo on launch day and are having second thoughts about keeping Apple's first foldable iPhone, tomorrow could be your last chance to return it for a refund.


Apple officially launched the iPhone Duo on Friday, October 23, so the standard 14-day return window for customers who purchased and received the device that day expires on Friday, November 6.

Apple's U.S. return policy, customers have 14 calendar days from receiving a product to return it, whether they purchased it online or at an Apple retail store. A similar standard return period applies in the UK and across much of the rest of Europe.

Apple's Canadian return policy, buyers have 15 calendar days from receiving their device to initiate a return, so if you got your device on launch day then you have until Saturday, November 7 to return it.

UK and EU Online Customers Have More Time to Send It Back

There's an important distinction to note if you're in the UK or the European Union and you purchased your iPhone Duo online. Under consumer protection laws, you have 14 days from receiving the device to notify Apple that you intend to return it. Once you've made that notification, you have a further 14 days to send the device back or arrange a collection.

November 20 to dispatch it. This also applies to devices ordered online and collected at an Apple Store. However, if you actually purchased your device directly at a physical Apple Store – which probably means you waited in a separate line to collections – then you generally need to return it within the initial 14-day window.

Note that the November 6 deadline doesn't apply to everyone who pre-ordered the iPhone Duo. Apple's return period is calculated from when customers received their devices, rather than when they placed their orders, so if your iPhone Duo arrived after launch day, you have more time to return it for a refund – if that's your preference.

What to Know Before Returning Your iPhone Duo

Apple asks customers to return their devices with the original packaging and included accessories. Also, remember to disable Find My for the iPhone Duo before returning the device. Returns can be initiated through Apple's online Order Status page or, in the US, at an Apple retail store.

Keep in mind that these policies apply only to purchases made directly from Apple – if you bought an iPhone Duo through a carrier or third-party retailer, you'll be subject to that seller's return policy.

title: You don’t need a $3,000 MacBook to get Live Activities in your menu bar
content:
Macworld





One of the big selling points of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED is its inclusion of a Dynamic Island. The camera is just a tiny bit lower and surrounded by display, so instead of a notch, you get an island that’s smaller but just as capable as the iPhone’s. When you run apps with Live Activities on the new laptop, they’ll populate the Dynamic Island, and you can tap or click on them to expand it. 
What iPhone users have enjoyed for years finally comes to Apple’s most expensive laptop. But it turns out, the Live Activities feature is coming to all Macs. In the macOS 27.3 beta, every Mac gets Live Activities. It’s just for some of Apple’s apps right now, such as Music and Clock, and some system functions like Screen Recording.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Live Activities in macOS 27.3 will appear in the menu bar as small ovals to the left of your icons, just as if there were a camera hole up there. When expanded, a small arrow appears that can be clicked to minimize it (see above). If you run several at a time, they’ll appear as separate instances next to each other. 
Third-party developers can now start implementing Live Activities in their macOS apps, which was already announced. However, what we thought was just in anticipation of the PROLED MacBook Pro turns out to be a new, useful feature for everyone.

title: 'Super Mario Odyssey' Can Now Run on Apple TV Thanks to AI
content:
A Reddit user was able to get Nintendo's "Animal Crossing: New Horizons" and "Super Mario Odyssey" to run natively on the Apple TV 4K, continuing a string of ports made possible with the use of AI (via Engadget).


TVPort, Reddit user FloatingFalafel's open-source project, is a fork of the nxnative toolkit used to recompile Switch and Switch 2 games for the Apple TV using a Mac. It was built using Claude Opus 5.5.

"Super Mario Odyssey" runs at 60fps according to FloatingFalafel, and "Animal Crossing" runs at 30fps. Other games haven't been tested, but the creator says people are welcome to use the open-source software to get other games to run. Game files are not included, and users will need to supply files from their own game cartridges, which requires a modified Nintendo Switch.

title: How 'Resident Evil' Director Zach Cregger Uses His iPhone to Make Movies
content:
Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak today shared an Apple TV video that offers a look at how "Resident Evil" director Zach Cregger uses an iPhone during filmmaking.


Cregger said he uses his iPhone and the Cadrage app to plan out filming sequences ahead of time. He decides what shots to take, what lenses to use for each shot, and what's in each frame. He then prints out the images so the crew knows exactly what to do.

According to Cregger, he used this process for "Weapons" and "Barbarian," two movies that he wrote and directed. He said every scene in those films was planned with photos in advance.

title: Apple Will Check Public iCloud Links for Harmful Content Starting in iOS 27.3
content:
Apple says it will start checking public iCloud links for harmful content in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3.


Images in iCloud Photos and files in iCloud Drive shared using the "Anyone with the link" option will be "made accessible to Apple" for a content check. Apple doesn't define harmful content, but it could mean malware, malicious files, and/or child sexual abuse material (CSAM) given Apple's mention of law enforcement involvement.
If you try to upload harmful content, Apple reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time. Apple may also take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement.

iCloud files can be shared with "Send a Copy," which sends a file directly, or "Share a Link," which lets someone download it. Link sharing options are "People you choose" or "Anyone with the link," and it's only the latter option that will be evaluated by Apple.

Apple does not say whether links created before the 27.3 updates will be checked.

Apple says content made available to anyone is no longer end-to-end encrypted, even when Advanced Data Protection is on.

title: Four no more: macOS 27.3 kills off those stupidly insecure certificates
content:
In the wake of the shockingly insecure security certificate fiasco, Apple has now completely blocked the compromised eMudhra certificates in macOS 27.3.


The security certificates were far from secure. 
In October, security researchers discovered that a number of certificates issued by one certificate authority were woefully insecure, to an obscene degree. While Apple has worked to block the certificates from being used, the current developer beta round goes one stage further.
After the discovery of the astoundingly weak certificates, Apple was able to stop the affected certificates from being used on iOS, iPadOS, and its other operating systems. However, as the curl utility in macOS doesn't check revocation information, Macs that had previously trusted the certificates would continue to do so, despite Apple's measures.

title: macOS 27.3 Includes an Important Security Fix
content:
The first macOS 27.3 developer beta includes an important security fix that prevents command-line tools from accepting eMudhra's compromised web certificates. Specifically, the update removes the affected certificates from the /etc/ssl/cert.pem file.


macOS 27.3 is not expected to be released to the public until December, but a macOS 27.2.1 update will likely arrive sooner with the same security fix.

support document related to this matter.

If you do not use command-line tools via Terminal or similar, you are already fully protected. Apple said it has been blocking eMudhra's compromised TLS web certificates since October 19 in Safari, Mail, and other apps that use Apple's networking and security frameworks, across all of its software platforms. The certificates are blocked automatically with no software update required, so most users do not need to take any action.

security researcher last month discovered that private cryptographic keys associated with eight of Indian company eMudhra's intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates were weak. The compromised keys could have allowed attackers to impersonate legitimate websites, potentially putting users' sensitive information at risk. So far, no evidence has surfaced that indicates the keys were exploited maliciously.

Apple’s HomePod and HomePod mini are obvious choices for Apple users, but there are plenty of alternatives that work with your iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple TV. Whether you want a compact kitchen speaker, a multi-room setup or a stereo system for music and TV, you could find features and value that better suit your needs.
AirPlay makes it easy to stream audio from your iPhone, iPad or Mac to a compatible wireless speaker, while AirPlay 2 lets you play music across multiple rooms. You can listen to your own music library or stream from Apple Music, Spotify and other services. We explain how AirPlay works and what it offers later in this guide.
Our picks cover a range of designs, features and budgets to help you choose the best speaker for your Apple devices. For Apple Music and Siri, start with the HomePod mini 2 or choose the full-size HomePod for richer sound. The Audio Pro A28 W is a good option if you want separate stereo speakers and a TV connection, while the Sonos Era 300 is our pick for Dolby Atmos music.
AirPlay 2 support is a priority for the speakers in this roundup, particularly if you want to build a multi-room system. We also include portable options for listening around the house or away from home, clearly identifying which support AirPlay and which rely on Bluetooth so you can choose the right connection for the way you listen.

Our listening tests found warm strings and delicate electronic chimes on Madonna’s Frozen, followed by sharp percussion and an energetic guitar riff that kept the music moving.
Setup is straightforward: the JBL One app connects over Bluetooth, then prompts for your Wi-Fi password. Once connected, you can play Apple Music through AirPlay 2 without returning to JBL’s app. Bluetooth provides another playback option, while built-in Alexa handles voice requests. There’s a switch to disable the microphone if you prefer.
Available in black or white, the M1 measures 184mm high and 125mm wide and deep, making it easy to accommodate on a desk or shelf. Three tweeters and a 105mm woofer fit inside. It requires mains power, so it’s suited to moving between rooms rather than taking out. Connections include dual-band Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, but there’s no 3.5mm or USB-C audio input.
Consider it over a HomePod mini if you want Bluetooth playback, Alexa or integration with JBL’s MK2 soundbars. Two M1s can form a stereo pair, and multiroom playback is supported. HomePod 2 offers Dolby Atmos and built-in Siri; the M1 is a compact alternative if those features matter less than connection flexibility and expanding a JBL system.

Two Era 300s widen stereo separation, while TV surround use requires a compatible Sonos soundbar. A single Era 300 isn’t a standalone Atmos soundbar replacement.

							
		
How to choose an AirPlay speaker
There’s a lot to think about when buying an AirPlay speaker so make sure you read this buying advice before splashing the cash.
Music streaming & compatibility
Having your favorite music follow you around your home is great, but conventional multi-room speakers often have significant limitations. Many, for example, will only work with a limited number of streaming services that are built into the apps provided by each manufacturer.
As you might expect, most will work with Spotify, while Tidal and Deezer also get a lot of support. But for some reason, Sonos is one of the few manufacturers of multi-room speakers that also supports Apple Music. In fact, some speakers only provide apps for iOS or Android mobile devices, which means that you can’t even play music from a Mac.
The other big problem with conventional speakers in the past was that you have generally had to buy them all from one manufacturer when assembling a multi-room setup because rival speakers were incompatible and wouldn’t work together.
AirPlay vs AirPlay 2
The speaker market changed dramatically in 2018 with the release of Apple’s updated AirPlay 2 software. Released to coincide with the original HomePod launch, AirPlay 2 has also been licensed to a number of well-known manufacturers, which means there’s now a wide range of compatible speakers available. In fact, every model in our top 10 works with AirPlay 2.
The first version of AirPlay, released back in 2010, was like a souped-up version of Bluetooth, allowing you to stream audio from any app on your Mac or iOS devices to any AirPlay-compatible speaker and freeing you from reliance on the manufacturer’s apps. AirPlay also uses a Wi-Fi connection, which means a higher bandwidth than Bluetooth and better sound quality – not to mention longer range.
The simplicity and versatility of AirPlay is great, but – like Bluetooth – its original version was only designed to work with one speaker at a time. AirPlay 2 takes Apple into the multi-room market, with the ability to stream music to several speakers in different rooms. (Alternatively, you can 
create a HomePods stereo pair in the same room.)
But the real game-changer with AirPlay 2 was interoperability, the ability to link together speakers from different manufacturers for the very first time. This means you can mix and match speakers around your home – picking, for instance, a HomePod as your main living-room speaker, a Sonos in the bedroom, and a portable speaker for drinks in the garden – and have them all linked up to play music simultaneously.

				
					

				
			
Which version of AirPlay is supported?
The important thing to remember is that there are now two types of AirPlay speaker. Some older models will use the original version of AirPlay – which is limited to streaming music to one speaker at a time – but new speakers (and certainly all the speakers in this article) focus on AirPlay 2. Some will have the AirPlay logo on the packaging, but this doesn’t specify whether it’s AirPlay or AirPlay 2. It’s therefore important to check which version is supported by any speaker before buying.
Given that AirPlay 2 has been around for three years, it would be surprising to see a manufacturer release an AirPlay 1 speaker right now, but it doesn’t hurt to check. You don’t want to get caught out.
It’s also worth mentioning that some older AirPlay speakers can be upgraded to work with AirPlay 2 as well. Libratone’s new Zipp 2 uses AirPlay 2, but it’s possible to download a software update for the older first-generation Zipp speakers that adds support for AirPlay 2. Unfortunately, that’s not the case with all AirPlay speakers, and some models are stuck with basic AirPlay.
Sound Quality vs Price
The fact that Apple licenses both AirPlay and AirPlay 2 to other manufacturers has other advantages too. Namely, the option to choose from a wide range of (often lower-cost) third-party speakers from companies like Sonos and Ikea.
At the other extreme, some really expensive hi-fi systems in the pipeline offer AirPlay 2 support for audiophiles and home cinema buffs. These options give you flexibility: you can spend heavily on a really high-quality speaker for your living room, for example, while opting for a less expensive model in the kitchen.
Indoors vs Outdoors
Some manufacturers provide more specialised speakers too, such as soundbars that you can use with your TV, or sub-woofers that can provide a bass boost for parties, or for sound effects when watching films.
Some even include rechargeable batteries and lightweight, portable designs so you can pick them up and carry them from room to room – which is certainly cheaper than buying a new speaker for each room – or take them out into the garden for a barbecue.
Connectivity
Connectivity is another key issue. The HomePod has been criticised for relying on Wi-Fi for streaming, with no option for quick and easy Bluetooth streaming for Android and other non-Apple devices. It doesn’t have a 3.5mm audio connector either, which would allow you to use it with a CD player or other audio devices.
Fortunately, many AirPlay and AirPlay 2 speakers provide a greater range of connectivity, allowing you to play music from a wider range of devices than the HomePod. Sonos has even announced it will be releasing an AirPlay 2 amplifier soon that can form the centrepiece of a serious home entertainment system.
In other words, AirPlay 2 is here to stay.
Bluetooth only options 
We’ve reviewed a few Bluetooth-only speakers that don’t offer AirPlay, but are still good options to consider, especially if you are looking for something portable:
Beats Pill

The Beats Pill suits listeners who want a portable speaker for camping, barbecues and days by the pool. Our reviewer found it reasonably loud and good-sounding below maximum volume, but bass lacks depth and heavy processing makes music sound constrained when pushed. It’s better suited to casual outdoor listening than critical listening at home.
Apple Music plays from your phone over Bluetooth or through USB-C, which also supports lossless audio. Basic playback and volume controls are straightforward, but powering off and pairing two Pills require less obvious button combinations. Our reviewer found these controls confusing and noted that the Android Beats app provides more help than iPhone settings.
The bottle-shaped enclosure fits wherever you might carry a water bottle, while a silicone covering helps protect against knocks. Its IP67 rating provides water and dust resistance. Beats claims up to 24 hours of battery life; our reviewer didn’t complete a rundown test but comfortably managed an afternoon at substantial volume. USB-C handles charging and can also top up your phone.
Choose the Pill over a HomePod mini for battery-powered outdoor use, rather than home multiroom listening: it lacks Wi-Fi and AirPlay. Two Pills can play in stereo or share playback in Amplify mode. HomePod 2 is the better fit for a permanent indoor system with fuller sound, Dolby Atmos and built-in Siri. Buy the Pill for portability, durability and endurance.

The Beosound A1 suits listeners who want a compact, durable speaker for travel, beach trips and outdoor gatherings. Our reviewer found its midrange powerful and precise, with clear vocals, firm percussion and enough energy for demanding rock tracks. High frequencies occasionally get lost in busy arrangements, however, and the deepest bass lacks the impact of larger speakers.
Apple Music plays from your phone over Bluetooth, with AAC support for Apple devices and aptX Adaptive for compatible Android hardware. There’s also USB-C audio, allowing a laptop to play music through the speaker while charging it. It has no Wi-Fi or AirPlay, so it won’t join an AirPlay multiroom system. 
Measuring 46mm high and 133mm across, and weighing 576g, the aluminum enclosure slips into a bag. A rubber base helps prevent slipping, and a leather wrist strap makes carrying easier. Its IP67 rating protects against dust and immersion in one meter of water for 30 minutes. Battery life is rated at 24 hours at medium volume, although a carrying case isn’t included.
Choose the A1 over a HomePod mini if outdoor use, battery endurance and wired laptop playback justify the extra expense. HomePod 2 makes more sense for a permanent indoor system where fuller sound, Dolby Atmos, Siri and multiroom playback matter most. The A1’s appeal is taking your music with you.




How we test speakers at Macworld 
We test speakers in home environments to assess how they perform in everyday use. Our reviews cover design and build quality, ease of setup, sound quality and additional features, with the emphasis varying depending on the type of speaker.
For sound quality, we listen for detail, clarity and tonal balance, including how naturally voices and instruments are reproduced. We pay particular attention to bass performance, especially with smaller speakers, assessing whether it lacks weight or overwhelms the rest of the sound. Most listening takes place at moderate volumes, but we also turn speakers up to check for distortion.
We assess how easily each speaker connects to an audio source and whether that connection remains stable during use. Where a companion app is available, we consider how straightforward it is to navigate and use the speaker’s features.
For smart speakers, we also test how reliably they recognize and respond to voice commands. Our recommendations draw on this hands-on testing and our reviewers’ experience, taking account of each speaker’s price, features and intended use.

title: Is It Worth Buying a Titanium Apple Watch?
content:
The Apple Watch Series 12's titanium option offers a premium metallic finish and sapphire crystal, sitting between the more affordable aluminum model and the higher-priced ceramic version. Is it worth choosing?


The titanium Apple Watch starts at $699, compared to $399 for aluminum. Available in Natural and Radiant Gold with a polished finish, it offers a more traditional watch aesthetic than the matte aluminum models. There are designer Apple Watch Hermès options too.

Ceramic Shield 2, replacing the Ion-X glass used on previous generations. Titanium is heavier than aluminum, so buyers who prioritize a lightweight watch for workouts and sleep tracking may prefer the cheaper option.

The titanium models also include cellular connectivity as standard, while aluminum models offer a choice of GPS or GPS and Cellular. The $300 difference between their starting prices therefore covers more than the case material and front crystal; if you already intend to buy a cellular Apple Watch, the additional cost of choosing titanium is smaller.

Titanium pairs particularly well with premium bands such as Apple's Link Bracelet or Milanese Loop. Its polished finish gives it a dressier appearance, although it can still be paired with rubber or woven bands for workouts and everyday use. For buyers who wear their Apple Watch throughout the day, including in formal settings, this versatility may be the best reason to pay more.

Internally, the titanium Apple Watch Series 12 offers the same chip, sensors, display technology, and battery life as the aluminum and ceramic versions. Paying more for titanium does not unlock additional features.

Ceramic's return means titanium is no longer the only premium alternative to aluminum. The Series 12's Pearl White and Night Blue ceramic cases also feature sapphire front crystal, so scratch resistance alone is not a reason to choose titanium over ceramic. Titanium is lighter than ceramic and offers a metallic appearance that may be easier to match with metal bracelets, while ceramic provides a more striking look, particularly in Pearl White.

Most customers will struggle to justify the extra cost of titanium. It is worth considering if you particularly want its polished metallic finish and sapphire crystal, especially if you were already planning to buy a cellular model. If you mainly want the polished finish and sapphire crystal, a discounted titanium Series 10 or Series 11 may also be worth considering.

Apple Watch Ultra 4. For another $100, the Ultra offers longer battery life and a more rugged design. The titanium Series 12 makes more sense if you want a premium Apple Watch with slimmer proportions and a more traditional appearance.

title: Does HomePod Mini 2 Have Improved Sound? Here's What Reviews Say
content:
Apple's press release for the HomePod mini 2 last month touted "rich sound" and "advanced computational audio," but it did not explicitly mention if the second-generation model has better sound compared to the original. A few early reviews of the speaker, however, said that audio quality has in fact improved.


Apple's tech specs pages for both the HomePod mini 2 and the original HomePod mini mention a "full-range driver" and "dual passive radiators for deep bass and crisp high frequencies," so the core speaker hardware is seemingly unchanged. However, the HomePod mini 2 is equipped with a much newer S10 chip that could use advanced algorithms to optimize sound in an improved manner compared to the S5 chip in the original model.

CNET's Tyler Lacoma said the HomePod mini 2 has "much better sound" than the original model.

Playing the same audio at the same volume on each speaker, I repeatedly switched between them while streaming Apple Lossless audio via Apple Music. The results were always the same: The new Mini 2 had significantly greater range and louder, clearer audio than the first HomePod Mini. It wasn't just noticeable: It was a big enough difference to completely change my mind about a speaker that didn't seem worth it on paper. If you want sound that can actually fill a room without losing quality, the HomePod Mini 2 is by far the preferable pick.
Cult of Mac's Ed Hardy said likewise:
To my ears, the second-gen version sounds noticeably better. Especially the stronger bass. I did a side-by-side comparison with HomePod mini 2 and my original model, and the new model definitely came out ahead.
Another benefit of the S10 chip that Apple did not emphasize: Siri is apparently much faster for basic requests such as playing a song and smart home commands, according to The Verge's Jennifer Pattison Tuohy. However, this is based on what Apple now calls Siri Classic, as the more intelligent and personalized Siri AI will not be available on the HomePod mini 2 until a future software update, according to Apple.

The Mini 2 is so much faster than the first-gen Mini, playing music in a few seconds and responding to smart home commands just as quickly. If you're fed up with standing over your HomePod waiting for it to finally do what you asked, then that alone is worth the upgrade.
The new HomePod mini was released last week, with U.S. pricing set at $149.

title: Best Apple Watch 2026: Series 12 vs Ultra 4 vs SE 3

Choosing the right Apple Watch depends on your budget, lifestyle and which features matter most to you. As of September 2026, Apple’s lineup consists of the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch SE 3, although the various combinations of case size, material, color and band can make choosing one seem like a bit of a minefield.
The Apple Watch Series 12 is the best choice for most people, combining a tougher display and more advanced heart-rate sensing with an S11 chip and 24-hour battery life. The larger and more rugged Apple Watch Ultra 4 is designed for endurance sports and outdoor adventures, offering precision GPS, diving features and up to 50 hours of battery life. The Apple Watch SE 3 remains the best-value option for buyers who want the core Apple Watch experience and can live without features such as ECG and the latest health sensors.
Apple updated the Series and Ultra models in September 2026, but the SE was unchanged. However, the SE 3 only arrived in 2025 and includes significant improvements over its predecessor, including an always-on display, temperature sensing and the same S10 chip found in the Series 11. You may also find older models at a discount, but check that the saving is worthwhile and bear in mind that watchOS 27 no longer supports every older Apple Watch. In this guide, we’ll explain the differences between the current models and help you decide whether you need to spend more on the Series 12 or Ultra 4 – or whether the SE 3 offers everything you need. We’ll compare their features, specifications and prices, as well as explain the choices of sizes, case materials, colors and bands, so you can buy the Apple Watch that best suits your needs.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s mainstream premium smartwatch and the best choice for most people. Its S11 chip powers a redesigned heart-rate sensor system that measures your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day. It also enables Audio Intelligence features including Sound Recognition, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are available to test in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta, released on November 3, 2026. Both initially support English.
The design remains familiar, but Apple has introduced new finishes: Light Gold and Dark Bronze replace Silver and Rose Gold on aluminum models, while Radiant Gold replaces Gold on titanium versions. Ceramic cases also return in Night Blue and Pearl White. Prices still start at $399, although some configurations cost more than their Series 11 equivalents.
Key advantages and limitations
Aluminum models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple claims is 60 percent more durable than the Ion-X glass used on the aluminum Series 11. Apple claims battery life remains at 24 hours, but outdoor workout tracking increases to 10 hours and the watch can charge to 80 percent in around 30 minutes.
In our Apple Watch Series 12 review, we recorded 51 and 40 hours of battery life across two runs – an average of 45.5 hours, compared with 47.5 hours for Series 11. Charging also varied: our Apple Watch Series 12 reached 58% and 72% after 30 minutes in separate tests, falling short of Apple’s claimed 80%. These results show that endurance can comfortably exceed Apple’s 24-hour rating, but they don’t demonstrate a consistent improvement over Series 11. Actual battery life depends on usage.
In the watchOS 27.3 developer beta, Live Rewind displays the previous 15 seconds of speech as text when you double-press the Digital Crown. However, assigning that gesture to Live Rewind means the traditional App Switcher is no longer available, making multitasking less convenient. The Series 12 also lacks the Ultra 4’s satellite connectivity, 50-hour battery life and brighter, more rugged display.
Who should buy the Apple Watch Series 12?
The Series 12 is the best option for anyone who wants Apple’s latest health and smart features without the size or price of the Ultra 4. Its advanced heart-rate sensing, Readiness score, tougher display and relatively compact design make it particularly attractive to health-conscious users and anyone upgrading from a Series 9 or older.
The new health features make Series 12 worth considering, but our review found variable battery life and charging, plus occasional sluggishness. Compare a discounted Series 11 if those health upgrades are not essential to you.
Who shouldn’t buy one?
Series 10 and 11 owners probably won’t gain enough to justify upgrading, especially because the quoted 24-hour battery life is unchanged. Outdoor adventurers who need satellite connectivity, extended workout tracking or maximum battery life should consider the Ultra 4 instead.
Should I buy an older version of the Apple Watch Series?
A discounted Series 10 or 11 could offer better value if you don’t need the new health sensing or Audio Intelligence features. The Series 9 is also still compatible with watchOS 27. Avoid the Series 8 and older models unless they are exceptionally cheap, because they cannot run watchOS 27 and will miss out on future feature updates.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is Apple’s most rugged and capable smartwatch, designed for endurance athletes and outdoor adventurers. It retains the Ultra 3’s 49mm titanium case, 3,000-nit display, Action button, dual-frequency GPS, satellite connectivity, 100-meter water resistance and recreational diving support.
Inside, the new S11 processor powers the redesigned heart-rate sensing system also found in the Series 12. It measures heart rate every five seconds throughout the day and enables Audio Intelligence features including Sound Recognition, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind and Siri Recap still pending are currently in the developer beta of watchOS 27.3.
Key advantages and limitations
Battery life is the Ultra 4’s biggest improvement, increasing from 42 to 50 hours under normal use. Extended Workout mode provides up to 25 hours with full GPS and heart-rate measurements, while Max Extended Workout mode can track outdoor runs and walks for up to 45 hours. Charging is faster too, with a 15-minute charge providing up to 18 hours of use.
Satellite connectivity, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving support and the bright display make it particularly well suited to demanding environments. However, its 49mm case is large and heavy, while charging to 80 percent takes around 45 minutes, compared with approximately 30 minutes for the Series 12. The external design is also largely unchanged. Pricing remains at $799, twice the Series 12’s starting price.
Who should buy the Apple Watch Ultra 4?
Choose the Ultra 4 if you need the longest Apple Watch battery life, highly accurate GPS, satellite connectivity, diving support or extended workout tracking. It is particularly suited to runners, hikers, cyclists, divers and anyone who regularly spends more than a day away from a charger.
Its extended battery life could also appeal to travelers and people working long shifts, even if they don’t participate in extreme sports.
Who shouldn’t buy one?
Most people will be better served by the smaller and less expensive Series 12. It provides the same S11 processor, redesigned heart-rate sensing and principal Audio Intelligence features without the Ultra’s bulk or $799 price. If you don’t need satellite communication, precision GPS, diving support or exceptionally long workout tracking, you are unlikely to benefit from the additional expense.
Should I buy an older Apple Watch Ultra?
The Ultra 3 remains a strong alternative if substantially discounted, although its battery lasts up to 42 rather than 50 hours. The Ultra 2 is the oldest model compatible with watchOS 27 and may also be worth considering at the right price, but it lacks some newer connectivity and battery improvements. Avoid the original Ultra unless it is exceptionally inexpensive, because it cannot run watchOS 27.

The Apple Watch SE 3 is Apple’s most affordable smartwatch and the best-value model in the current lineup. Introduced in September 2025, it brought substantial improvements over the SE 2, including an always-on display, the S10 processor used by the Series 11, temperature sensing, fast charging and 64GB of storage.
It also supports Double Tap and Wrist Flick gestures, on-device Siri and media playback through its speaker. The aluminum case comes in Midnight or Starlight, but there is no longer a Silver option. Prices start at $249/£219, although it can fall as low as $199 during sales.
Key advantages and limitations
The SE 3 provides the essential Apple Watch experience, including fitness and sleep tracking, Sleep Score, heart-rate alerts, temperature-based cycle tracking, sleep apnea notifications, Fall Detection and Crash Detection. Its Ion-X display glass is four times more crack-resistant than that of the SE 2, while cellular versions add 5G connectivity.
Battery life remains limited to 18 hours, although Low Power Mode extends this to 32 hours. Fast charging reaches approximately 80 percent in 45 minutes, and a 15-minute charge provides around eight hours of use. The SE 3 lacks ECG, Blood Oxygen monitoring, hypertension notifications and the redesigned Health Sensing System found on the Series 12. Its 1,000-nit display, thicker bezels and limited material choices also make it feel less premium.
Who should buy the Apple Watch SE 3?
The SE 3 is ideal for first-time Apple Watch buyers and anyone who wants fitness tracking, notifications and safety features without paying for advanced health sensors. It is also a strong option for children when using the cellular model with Family Setup, and for older users who could benefit from Fall Detection, Emergency SOS and heart-rate monitoring.
Who shouldn’t buy one?
Choose the Series 12 instead if you want ECG, Blood Oxygen monitoring, hypertension notifications, more advanced heart-rate sensing or a brighter, more premium display. Buyers who need multi-day battery life, satellite connectivity or specialist outdoor features should consider the Ultra 4.
Should I buy an older Apple Watch SE?
No. The SE 2 cannot run watchOS 27 and lacks the SE 3’s always-on display, temperature sensing, faster charging, newer gestures and additional storage. Even at a substantial discount, its reduced software lifespan makes it difficult to recommend in 2026.  

							
		


watchOS 27 features: What’s new and what requires Series 12 or Ultra 4
Apple released a new version of the software that runs on the Apple Watch – watchOS 27 – on September 14, 2026, but not every new feature is available on every supported watch. Some improvements are software-led and work across compatible models, while others depend on the S11 chip and redesigned sensors in the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
The hardware-dependent health features unique to the 2026 Watches include background heart-rate measurements every five seconds and HRV (heart rate variability) measurements every five minutes. The Series 12 and Ultra 4 also gain the Readiness app, which analyzes recent activity, training load, sleep and health data to produce a daily recovery score. Other exclusives include daytime resting heart-rate and HRV data in Vitals, a real-time chart in the Heart Rate app, more accurate all-day step counting and a Steps complication that updates on the watch face.
The S11 chip also enables Apple’s Audio Intelligence features. Automatic Music Recognition uses Shazam to identify nearby songs and display them in the Smart Stack, while Sound Recognition can detect doorbells, alarms, sirens and crying babies without relying on the iPhone. Live Rewind displays a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation after a double-press of the Digital Crown; it does not save an audio recording. Siri Recap produces high-level summaries of conversations. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are available to test with the watchOS 27.3 and iOS 27.3 developer betas, released November 3, 2026. These features require an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone 16 or later, excluding iPhone 16e. They initially support English and are not yet available in the EU.
Other watchOS 27 features are more widely available. These include the Dynamic App Grid, redesigned Find My app, menopause and perimenopause tracking, Call Context and Workout Buddy improvements. Apple has also introduced the Longevity section and Health Age.
Compatibility is considerably more restricted than it was with watchOS 26. Series 9 and Ultra 2 are now the oldest supported models, while the SE 3 is the only compatible SE. The Series 6, Series 7, Series 8, SE 2 and original Ultra cannot install watchOS 27. Anyone considering a discounted older Apple Watch should therefore choose a Series 9, Series 10, Series 11, Ultra 2 or Ultra 3 if receiving current feature updates is important. See: These Apple Watches are now obsolete.

Consider your wrist size and comfort
The watch should feel secure without dominating your wrist or restricting movement. The 40mm SE 3 is the best option for particularly small wrists, while the 42mm Series 12 provides a larger display in a case that remains manageable for most people. If possible, try both sizes in an Apple Store before buying.
Consider display size and readability
A larger screen makes text, notifications and onscreen controls easier to see and use. The 49mm Ultra 4 has the largest display, but its 63g titanium case is substantially heavier than the aluminum Series 12 or SE 3. The 46mm Series 12 offers a spacious display without the Ultra’s additional bulk.
Consider whether you need the Ultra
Don’t choose the Ultra 4 solely because it has the largest screen. Its size makes most sense if you also need its rugged titanium construction, satellite connectivity, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving support or 50-hour battery life. For everyday use, the Series 12 will generally be more comfortable.
Check band compatibility
Apple Watch bands aren’t universally interchangeable. Bands designed for smaller cases generally fit the 38mm, 40mm, 41mm and newer 42mm watches, while larger bands work with 44mm, 45mm, 46mm and 49mm models. However, the older 42mm case belongs to the larger band family, so check the compatibility information before reusing or ordering a band.


						

							


Aluminum, titanium or ceramic: Which Apple Watch material is best?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Another consideration when buying an Apple Watch is its case material, which affects its durability, weight, appearance and price. Apple currently offers aluminum, titanium and ceramic cases, although the available materials depend on the model.
Aluminum: Best for most people
Aluminum is the lightest and most affordable choice. It is the only material available for the Apple Watch SE 3 and the entry-level option for the Series 12, helping to keep their starting prices at $249 and $399 respectively.
It is a good choice for everyday wear, fitness and sleep tracking because it feels lighter on the wrist than the premium alternatives. The SE 3 uses Ion-X display glass, which Apple says is four times more crack-resistant than that of the SE 2. The aluminum Series 12 has the tougher Ceramic Shield 2 display, which Apple claims is 60 percent more durable than the Ion-X glass used by the aluminum Series 11.
Titanium: Best for premium durability
Titanium is available with the Series 12 and is the only case material offered with the Ultra 4. It provides a more premium finish and is paired with highly scratch-resistant sapphire crystal rather than the glass used on aluminum models.
The Series 12 titanium case is available in Natural or Radiant Gold. It is a good option for anyone who wants a more luxurious and durable everyday watch without moving up to the much larger Ultra.
The Ultra 4 uses a rugged Grade 5 titanium case in Natural or Black. It is designed for outdoor adventures, endurance sports and diving, with a 49mm case, 100-meter water resistance and recreational diving support. However, its size and 63g weight make it less comfortable for smaller wrists and sleep tracking.
Ceramic: Best for distinctive styling
Ceramic returns as a premium Series 12 option in Pearl White and Night Blue. It has a glossy, distinctive finish and uses a sapphire crystal display, but it is heavier and considerably more expensive than the aluminum version. The ceramic cases are also slightly larger than the other Series 12 configurations.
Which material is best for Apple Watch?
For most buyers, aluminum offers the best balance of price, durability and comfort. Choose titanium if you want a more premium finish, sapphire crystal or the Ultra 4’s specialized outdoor capabilities. Ceramic is primarily a style-led luxury choice for buyers who want the most distinctive Series 12 and are prepared to pay more for it.

For most people, the Sport Loop is the best all-round choice because it is light, breathable and easy to adjust. Its softness also makes it particularly comfortable for sleep tracking.
For workouts and swimming, choose a Sport Band or Nike Sport Band. The perforated Nike version provides better ventilation during intense exercise. Divers and regular swimmers should consider the Ocean Band, while runners and hikers may prefer the lighter Trail Loop or more rugged Alpine Loop.
For work or formal occasions, the Milanese Loop, Link Bracelet, Modern Buckle and Magnetic Link provide a smarter appearance. Apple’s Hermès collection offers the most luxurious—and most expensive—options.
Before buying, check that the strap supports your Apple Watch case size and wrist measurement. Solo Loop and Braided Solo Loop straps require particularly careful sizing because they cannot be adjusted with a clasp. Third-party straps can offer excellent value, but quality, fit and fastening security vary considerably.


Do I need a cellular Apple Watch?
Whether you need a cellular Apple Watch depends mainly on how often you plan to leave your iPhone behind. For most buyers, the answer is no: a GPS-only Apple Watch offers better value and can already do a great deal without an active connection to an iPhone.
Away from your iPhone, a GPS Apple Watch can still track workouts, monitor health, record location data, use Apple Pay and play music or podcasts downloaded to the watch. When connected to a known Wi-Fi network, it can also send and receive messages, make calls and use many online services. See our guide to Everything an Apple Watch can do without an iPhone.
Cellular becomes useful when you regularly leave your iPhone at home but still want calls, messages, music streaming, navigation and notifications. This makes it particularly valuable for runners, cyclists, swimmers and gym users who don’t want to carry a phone. It can also provide reassurance when you are walking alone or exercising away from Wi-Fi, because the watch can contact emergency services after a fall or crash using its own mobile connection.
A cellular model is also the right choice when setting up an Apple Watch for a child or older relative who doesn’t have an iPhone. Apple Watch For Your Kids, previously called Family Setup, allows a family member’s watch to be configured from another person’s iPhone. A cellular plan enables calls, messages and location sharing when the watch is away from the managing iPhone.
The drawbacks are cost and redundancy. A cellular Series or SE generally costs more than its GPS equivalent, and you must also pay your network provider a monthly fee. If your iPhone is nearly always in your pocket or bag, the watch will normally use its connection instead, leaving you paying for cellular service that you rarely need. See: I switched to a cellular Apple Watch to prove I didn’t need one.
Our recommendation: The Ultra 4 includes cellular as standard, so there is no GPS-only version. For the Series 12 and SE 3, choose cellular only if you expect to leave your iPhone behind regularly or need Family Setup. Otherwise, save your money and buy the GPS model. For a more detailed comparison, see The pros and cons of a cellular Apple Watch.


						

							


Can you use an Apple Watch without an iPhone?
Yes, but with important caveats. An Apple Watch can do a surprising amount without an iPhone nearby, but an iPhone is required for the initial setup and to manage some settings. You cannot set up an Apple Watch using a Mac, iPad or Android phone.
The exception is Apple Watch For Your Kids, previously called Family Setup. This allows a parent or guardian to use their iPhone to configure a cellular Apple Watch for a child or another family member who doesn’t have an iPhone of their own.
Once it has been set up, an Apple Watch can perform many tasks without its paired iPhone nearby – and some don’t require an internet connection at all. These include:
Tracking workouts and activity: Record runs, walks and other exercises, close Activity rings and collect GPS data. The results sync with the iPhone when it reconnects.
Monitoring health: Measure heart rate, track sleep, log medications and use other health features supported by the particular watch.
Playing downloaded media: Listen to music, podcasts and audiobooks stored on the watch using Bluetooth headphones.
Using Apple Pay: Make contactless payments without an iPhone or internet connection once Apple Pay has been configured.
Using offline tools: Set alarms and timers, use the stopwatch and compass, and view photos that have been synced to the watch.
Other features require either Wi-Fi or a cellular connection when the iPhone isn’t nearby. With an internet connection, the watch can make and receive calls, send messages, check email, stream music and podcasts, use Maps and access online apps and services.
Fall Detection and Crash Detection can recognize an incident without your iPhone nearby, but contacting emergency services requires a suitable connection. Most Apple Watches need cellular coverage or Wi-Fi calling with an internet connection. Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Ultra 4 also support Emergency SOS via satellite in supported countries and regions, including the U.S. and U.K. This allows emergency texting when cellular and Wi-Fi coverage are unavailable, and can relay automatic Fall Detection or Crash Detection alerts if you are unresponsive. Satellite connectivity requires being outdoors with a clear view of the sky and horizon.
An Apple Watch therefore cannot completely replace an iPhone, but it doesn’t need to remain beside it throughout the day. For a complete breakdown, read all the things an Apple Watch can do without an iPhone.


						

							


How we choose the best Apple Watch
Macworld’s Apple Watch recommendations draw on more than a decade of hands-on experience. Our writers have tested and reviewed every generation since the original Apple Watch, comparing each new model with both its current rivals and previous generations before deciding whether it deserves a recommendation.
Our assessment focuses on the factors that make a meaningful difference in everyday use:
Real-world testing: We assess comfort, build quality, display visibility, performance, battery life, charging, health sensors, fitness tracking and software features. We also consider how well the watch performs during everyday activities, workouts and sleep tracking—not simply how its specifications compare on paper.
Value and upgrade potential: A newer or more expensive Apple Watch is not automatically the best choice. We consider whether its improvements justify the price, whether owners of recent models would benefit from upgrading and whether a discounted previous-generation watch offers better value.
Honest recommendations: We clearly identify compromises such as limited battery life, missing health sensors, a bulky design or features that most people are unlikely to use. We don’t recommend a product simply because it has the most impressive specifications.
Advice for different buyers: There is no single Apple Watch that suits everyone. We recommend the Series 12 for most buyers, the SE 3 for those seeking the best value, and the Ultra 4 for endurance athletes and outdoor adventurers who need its longer battery life, rugged construction and specialist capabilities.
Our final recommendations therefore combine extensive testing, expert judgment, price analysis and practical buying advice. The aim is not merely to identify the Apple Watch with the longest feature list, but to help you find the model that provides the right balance of features, comfort and value for the way you will actually use it.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Is now a good time to buy an Apple Watch
Now is a good time to buy an Apple Watch because the brand-new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 went on sale on September 18, 2026. However, our recommendation is to wait for Black Friday sales towards the end of November for the best deals. See: Should I buy an Apple Watch now or wait? 





2.
What is the difference between the Series 12 and SE 3?
The Apple Watch Series 12 offers a brighter, tougher display, premium aluminum, titanium and ceramic cases, and the newer S11 chip. It also includes advanced health features such as ECG, Blood Oxygen monitoring, high-frequency heart-rate sensing and the Readiness app, plus exclusive Audio Intelligence features. Battery life is rated at 24 hours. 
The $249/£219 SE 3 uses the S10 chip, lasts 18 hours and provides essential fitness, sleep and safety features, but lacks the Series 12’s advanced sensors and premium materials.





3.
Can you swim while wearing an Apple Watch?
Yes, you can swim while wearing an Apple Watch, but the level of water resistance varies significantly depending on the model. The Apple Watch Ultra models are the most water-capable in the lineup. They are water-resistant to 100 meters and are suitable for swimming, snorkeling, scuba diving (up to 40 meters), and high-speed water sports. The Ultra models also include a depth gauge (up to 40 meters) and a water temperature sensor, making them a genuine companion for divers and endurance swimmers. 
Apple Watch Series 12, Series 11 and Series 10 are water-resistant to 50 meters and suitable for shallow-water activities such as swimming. They also support snorkeling to 6 meters, but should not be used for scuba diving, waterskiing or other high-velocity water sports. Water resistance can diminish over time.
The Apple Watch SE 3 is also water-resistant to 50 meters and is considered “swimproof”.
Follow these steps to enable Water Lock: 
Before swimming, press the side button to open Control Center. 
Tap the water-drop icon to enable Water Lock. 
After swimming press and hold the Digital Crown to unlock the screen and eject water from the speaker.





4.
Should I buy an old Apple Watch model?
Buying an older Apple Watch can be a great way to save money, but in late 2026, you need to be much more careful than in previous years. The biggest factor is software support, as watchOS 27 dropped support for several relatively recent models.
Apple made a significant change with watchOS 27. The update drops support for the Apple Watch SE 2, Series 6, Series 7, Series 8 and the original Apple Watch Ultra. If you want a watch that will continue to receive the latest features and security updates, you must buy a model with at least an S9 chip. This means the oldest supported models are now the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2, both from 2023. 
If you are shopping for an older Apple Watch our recommendation is to buy refurbished watches from Apple. Read Should I buy a refurbished Apple Watch? for guidance. Another good option is to look for previous-generation Apple Watch models in major sales events, such as Black Friday. Take a look at the best prices right now in the boxes below.

title: Apple May Phase Out Non-Touch High-End MacBook Pros
content:
Apple will likely consolidate its high-end MacBook Pro lineup around touchscreen models, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


Writing in his latest "Power On" newsletter, Gurman questioned whether Apple would keep updating its high-end ‌MacBook Pro‌ models without touchscreens. The company has retained the mini-LED M5 Pro and M5 Max models alongside the new touchscreen versions, which cost $400 more.

Gurman cited the resources required to support parallel product lines across development, production, and promotion. Given the price difference, he expects the two offerings to converge, although he did not specify when Apple might stop developing the non-touch models.

previously said the chip upgrade would arrive toward the end of 2027.

first reported plans for the redesigned base model in July, when he outlined a potential launch in the first half of 2027.

unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pros last week, retaining the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips introduced in March. The redesign pairs OLED displays and Dynamic Island with a lighter, slightly thinner enclosure and a revised cooling system that channels warm air away from the screen.

title: Apple's Lockdown Mode thwarted by a new persistent iPhone jailbreak
content:
A team of hackers has come up with a new jailbreak for the iPhone, demonstrating how it persists with Lockdown Mode on, even after an update to iOS 27.2.


Lockdown Mode on iPhone is for users facing grave threats to their digital security
Lockdown Mode is Apple's way to harden device security,  intended to protect high-profile individuals from sophisticated cyberattacks. While Apple claimed back in March 2026 that it had managed a 100% protection rate since 2022, it seems it's not completely impenetrable.
In a video posted to X, hacker group Calif shows an iPhone 18 Pro with Lockdown Mode enabled. A PDF is then sent to the iPhone using AirDrop and viewed.
