The iPhone Duo is very appropriately named, and not just because it has two screens, two rear cameras, two front cameras, and is shaped sort of like a capital “D”.
This is a phone of dichotomies, where each facet of the experience delivers something wonderful and exciting while also delivering something frustrating and backwards. For every aspect of the iPhone Duo that you can say something good about, there’s an “on the other hand…” that cuts the other way.
I find the iPhone Duo almost impossible to recommend to a casual buyer, and yet it’s the most fun I’ve had exploring a new iPhone in over a decade. It is simultaneously delightful and frustrating, big and small, useful and hindering, inviting and off-putting.
iPhone Duo: Performance and battery life
This might be an off place to start, but the iPhone Duo is so unique and has so many interesting facets that its performance and battery life are almost boring by comparison. So let’s get that out of the way first.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The Duo has the same A20 Pro chip as the iPhone 18 Pro, which as I noted in that review, is crazy fast. This is far and away the fastest folding phone you can buy.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




You can generally look at any benchmark result for the iPhone 18 Pro and just consider that the iPhone Duo will perform the same, with a two small caveats. First, 3D graphics benchmarks tend to run just a little slower on the Duo. It’s still faster than any prior iPhone and blows the doors off any other foldable, but the small difference was consistent in my testing.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Second, heat is a little bit more of an issue than with the iPhone 18 Pro. Yes, the Duo gets pretty hot during extended video-taking, gaming, or other intensive applications, but not hot enough to cause serious issues. It’s noticeable, though, and impacts performance a little bit more than when running the same tasks on an iPhone 18 Pro.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Our standard battery benchmark relies on an old app that crashed on launch on the Duo, so I can’t deliver strict comparison numbers. In a week of use, however, I can tell you that battery life is highly dependent on how often you use the big inner screen.
Play games or edit video with the big inner screen a lot, and you’ll be looking for the charger by mid-afternoon. Spend a lot more time with the device folded, and you’ll wrap up the day with plenty of battery to spare. It’s either one of the longest-lasting iPhones around, or a $2,000 phone that can’t even make it to sunset on a charge, depending on how you use it. There’s that “Duo” thing.
iPhone Duo: Cameras you’ll tolerate
The most expensive and ostensibly best iPhone in the world does not have the best cameras. For a start, it’s missing the telephoto camera you get on the Pro iPhones, but the camera issues go deeper than that.
The main  rear camera is good, but not as good as Apple’s latest on the iPhone 18 Pro–it’s about on par with an iPhone 17. The Ultra-wide camera is the same 48MP camera Apple has used since the iPhone 16 Pro, which is fine.
The selfie camera on the outside display is a 12MP camera that resembles the one on the iPhone 17e or earlier, but it has Center Stage and can zoom and rotate without rotating the iPhone, features that were previously only available on the superior 18MP selfie camera that was introduced with the iPhone 17.
The camera software experience isn’t what you get on Pro iPhones either. You can’t shoot ProRAW images or ProRes video, there’s no Log 2 gamma, no shutter speed or histogram. That seems like a ripoff in a $2,000 iPhone. But you do get the new Photographic Styles that give you control over grain and texture, and focus peaking, and white balance.

				
					

				
			The Duo cameras are serviceable, but missing Pro features you’d expect at this price.
Britta O’Boyle




Then there’s the inside FaceTime camera, which sits under the display behind a small circle you can easily spot because it doesn’t have the antireflective nano-texture over it. I quickly ignored this anomaly and soon hardly even noticed it’s there, but the atrocious quality of that camera is impossible to ignore. It’s got poor resolution, terrible clarity, and awful dynamic range, takes paltry 4MP images, and is saddled with all sorts of over-processing artifacts. It’s meant for video calling apps such as FameTime or Zoom, where it does an okay job since your streaming video is low-res and highly compressed anyway. But that does little to make me feel better about it.

The main camera (left) takes decent selfies, while the under-display inside camera (right) is a mess.



Thankfully, the outside display has a much better camera. It’s position in the corner is a fine solution, and the Dynamic Island’s move to a vertical orientation there is actually quite delightful. I’ve don’t know what engineering challenge prevented Apple from simply using a similar cutout camera with Dynamic Island on the inside display, but it would have provided for much better quality and would exactly mirror the outer display.

				
					

				
			The camera can do some neat tricks with the outside display.
Britta O’Boyle




Because it’s a folding phone, there are a few neat tricks up the Duo’s sleeve. A mode called “Smart Take” will watch the viewfinder for you and take a photo whenever the people in view are holding still and facing the camera, so you can easily take multiple shots where everyone is ready. It’s a good idea that should come to every iPhone.
You can also flip the viewfinder around to the outside screen even when the Duo is open, which will let you take a selfie with the 48MP main or ultra-wide camera. This gives you better selfie quality than any iPhone ever before, and when taking photos with the phone opened up, you can mirror the viewfinder to the outside screen so your subject can see themselves and strike a pose they’re happy with. If you’re trying to get a kid to look at the camera, Kid Cue plays a Snoopy animation on that screen to attract your child’s attention. These are all impressive and delightful features that show off how special this phone is.
There’s that Duo thing again. The camera hardware is frustratingly backward in some cases, and Pro features are missing, but there are some unique new capabilities you can’t get on any other iPhone that are genuinely useful. I’m okay with the cameras on the iPhone Duo, but I’m just okay with them, and that’s not what I want from a $2,000+ phone.
iPhone Duo: Two very unequal iPhones
I hear all the time from users who really wish Apple would make an iPhone mini again. It’s not so much that they were in love with the tiny screen, but rather that they were in love with the tiny phone, and were willing to deal with a small screen and lesser battery life for something so light, pocketable, and easy to use with one hand.
That’s why the Duo is so frustrating to use when it’s closed. The area of the outside screen occupied by apps is tiny, but the phone itself is thick, wide, fat, and heavy. It’s all the drawbacks of the iPhone mini and none of the benefits.
Open it up and you’re in a whole new world. The phone’s weight seems more appropriate for its size, and it’s nice and thin. The expansive screen looks wonderful. Apple’s nano-texture screen layer saps away a bit of contrast and “pop,” as with any matte display, but it’s still a beautiful screen. Plus that matte finish makes it much nicer to use outside where reflections are distracting.

				
					

				
			The crease is visible in the right light, but when the screen is on, the matte texture really hides it remarkably well.
Jason Cross / Foundry




The the main purpose of a n inside matte display may have been to hide the crease, which it does very well, but it also hides any minor smudges, scrapes, or other imperfections. Yes, a flexible screen with a nano-texture covering is not nearly as scratch-proof as a typical iPhone display, but it’s folded away and protected when the phone is in your pocket or bag.
The speakers are surprisingly good, with decent stereo separation and clarity. The bass is as poor as it is on any other iPhone, but this is a surprisingly good device to watch a TV show on.
One of the tradeoffs Apple had to make with the Duo is the removal of Face ID in favor of Touch ID, which is located in the side power button like non-Pro iPads. I still miss Face ID every day. Touch ID on old iPhones was always in the same place, so you built a muscle memory around tapping on the sensor. The same is true of Touch ID on a MacBook. However, since the iPhone Duo is meant to be used in four or five different “postures,” the side button’s location moves as you change the phone’s orientation. You can unlock your iPhone automatically if you’re wearing an Apple Watch, but that doesn’t help with the many times you authenticate with Touch ID to input a password or approve a purchase or download. I can live with Touch ID on this thing, but I don’t like it.
For $2,000, the iPhone Duo gives you two iPhones. One is a thick, heavy, wide, uncomfortable iPhone with a tiny glossy display. The other is a big, expansive, thin, beautiful iPhone with a nano-texture display. It’s that “Duo” thing all over again. Your enjoyment of the Duo is in direct proportion to how often you use it in the unfolded state, and to do that, you need the right apps.
iPhone Duo: The apps that make the phone
Developers are having a blast with the Duo, making fun little apps that don’t serve much purpose other than to make use of the unique capabilities of the hardware, just as they did in the early days of iPhone. Back then it was apps that make it look like you were drinking a beer or holding a flickering lighter, today it’s a faux-Walkman or digital panini press. These are silly gimmick apps that will be forgotten in time, but they recapture the fun of the first few years of iPhone, when developers were just making cool little toys and experiments for a buck just because they could.
Of course, apps that aren’t just gimmicks or toys can make great use of the larger inside screen, but they have to be updated for the Duo to do so. These Duo-optimized apps look and function differently. They show two views at once, or a persistent sidebar, an expansive map with an info overlay, or other “wouldn’t fit on a normal iPhone” layouts that truly make them better. They gracefully lsupport landscape or portrait views, and some even change layouts if the Duo is folded slightly like a book or folded over like a tent to show the outside screen proppep up on your desk.
From Slack to Netflix to Yelp and more, these apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later, and optimized for the Duo, are so nice to use, with interface elements along the right edge when you use the outside screen and thoughtful use of the expansive inside screen no matter how you hold your phone. Of course, nearly all of Apple’s apps have been Duo-optimized like this, though the Apple Store is curiously unoptimized, and Safari could use some interface tweaks to make it a little easier to use on the inside screen.

				
					

				
			Apps like Outlook make great use of the expansive inside display and are so much more productive than on a regular iPhone.
Foundry




Unfortunately, he majority of popular apps are not yet updated for the Duo, even more than a week after launch. Some, such as Gmail, TikTok, Reddit, or Google Maps, are built using the iOS 27.0 SDK and can therefore resize to mostly fill the inside display. But they don’t understand the size of the device they’re on so they don’t make practical use of the Duo. For example, my Gmail inbox is just stretched across the whole screen instead of showing folders and a reading panel, for example. It’s better than an app that doesn’t use the space at all, but next to other apps that treat the Duo properly, it’s still not great.
Worse, there are just scores of everyday apps that haven’t updated to the iOS 27 SDK yet, and just appear in an iPhone-shaped window in the middle of the screen with huge black bars around it. Turn the Duo to portrait orientation and it’ll float in the middle with black bars all around and a return of the old iPad “expand” button to double-size the app to fill the screen. But this is actually worse, because the interfaces are designed around a smaller-size device and become really cumbersome and hard to reach on an open iPhone Duo.
It’s an awful experience, and it stings all the more because you paid over $2,000 for it. And there are so many popular and oft-used apps in this category: Google Home, Ring, Uber, Teams, Snapchat, Hulu, nearly every popular mobile game, Venmo, Google Docs, Audible, almost all the credit card and banking apps… the list of “black-bar apps” goes on and on and includes scores of the top names.

				
					

				
			Using the Ring app as a tiny strip surrounded by black bars is a miserable experience.
Foundry




You can always run two apps side by side, wether they’re optimized for the Duo or not, and you can drag and drop content between them. It’s a simple and intuitive multitasking experience that requires absolutely no learning curve; it’s just like running two iPhones side by side. It makes me wish Apple would actually pare back the iPad multitasking experience to match. Sometimes less is more.

				
					

				
			Running two apps side-by-side on the Duo is intuitive and useful.
Foundry




The situation is changing rapidly, and apps are being updated all the time. Works on Duo is my favorite crowdsourced database to keep informed. The site’s readiness report currently shows just 34 percent of the top 100 apps are either optimized specifically for the Duo or at least run full screen on the inside display. That could double and you would still run into black bars every day! The gaming situation is even worse at only 14 percent of the top 100 games properly running full screen.
The “Duo” principle strikes again: Optimized apps gives you exciting new ways to work and play but every other app is actually worse on the Duo than on any other iPhone.
iPhone Duo: Durability and reliability
Durability is a top concern for buyers of Apple’s first folding phone, especially considering the price. At this point, you should not be surprised to hear it’s another good news/bad news situation.
The good news is that the iPhone Duo is IP68 rated for dust and water ingress, while nearly all other folding phones are IP48 and more sensitive to dust and dirt. Apple’s matte nano-texture coating on the inside display also hides micro scratches an imperfections really well. Obviously any phone with a mechanical hinge and folding glass is going to be more sensitive to rough handling and strenuous environments than a standard iPhone. Clear any dirt away before you work the hinge, because you can absolutely ruin it if enough grit gets in there.
It’s far too soon to see if there are long-term problems, but early tests using machines to open and close the hinge tens of thousands of times show that it holds up just fine and the crease does not get meaningfully worse. It’s impressive engineering. In many ways, the iPhone Duo is more durable than most other folding phones, though clearly must be handled more carefully than a typical modern iPhone. That’s just one of the tradeoffs inherent to folding phones.

				
					

				
			A disturbing number of Duo owners are reporting that their screens break, in the same place, under normal operation.
Midnight_Slump / Reddit




Then there’s the other side. Users are reporting defects that cause the inner display to break thanks to a potential defect in the hinge design or manufacture, and it’s widespread enough to get comment from Apple. And no matter how good that inner display is, it definitely does scratch more easily than the outer display so you’ll want to keep it away from keys, coins, and the like.
Apple will repair or replace iPhone Duos with the screen/hinge defect as you would expect, but in general, repair of the Duo is very expensive. For example, repairing the inner display will cost you $999, half the price of the whole phone. So I definitely recommend AppleCare+ ($20/month or $200/year) if you’re spending all that money on a Duo, which will bring the cost of an inner display repair down to $99. 
The iPhone is new again
Folding phones intrinsically carry with them some tradeoffs that some users would rather not make, and on top of those, Apple has made some design decisions that not everyone will be happy with. Add on a constantly changing app optimization situation and you have an iPhone that takes a certain amount of tolerance to enjoy.
At the same time, it’s refreshingly new; perhaps the first truly new iPhone since the original. This is the first time since those very early days where apps truly behave differently; not just slightly taller or higher-res, but functionally different. My time with the iPhone Duo has been filled with discovery. Apps I hadn’t considered before are worth a look simply because of how they have been “Duo-fied,” and some of my old mainstays feel fresh and new.
On the other hand, this is the first iPhone I’ve ever used where a great many of the apps I rely on every day just aren’t as good as they are on my old phone. Small and awkward on the outside screen, and centered (or stretched) on the inside screen with black bars and interface elements that are hard to reach. I can’t imagine paying $2,000 or more for an iPhone that is worse than my old one, but there are times when that is definitely true.
Even for those who are accepting of folding phone compromises, it feels like the iPhone Duo is not ready yet. Apple has a little bit of work to do on its own apps and OS, but more importantly, there are thousands of popular apps that need to be updated to provide a decent experience. And there’s nothing they can do that will make that inside selifie camera good. The iPhone Duo is not for everyone, and not just because its price puts it out of reach. It just imposes a set of compromises around durability, cameras, and usability that some people won’t want to make. Some people are just not folding phone people.
It remains to be seen how quickly most of these issues will be worked out, and one can’t review a device based on its unrealized potential and promise. That’s why, even though I’m having more fun exploring the iPhone Duo than I have any new iPhone in over a decade, I can’t really recommend anyone buy one. Yet.

title: Best MacBook Neo accessories: Chargers, hubs, stands and more
content:
Macworld





The MacBook Neo, Apple’s entry-level laptop officially announced in early March 2026, is a sensation, bringing the Mac to a whole new market with its low price but surprisingly powerful specs and features. For just $699 you get the full Mac experience in a premium aluminum 13-inch laptop with FaceTime HD camera, speakers, mic and two USB-C ports.
Compared to similarly priced Windows laptops and iPads with keyboards, the MacBook Neo offers superior build quality, performance, and storage capacity—for hundreds of dollars less than any previous Mac laptop.
We’ve outlined some of the small compromises that Apple has made to get to that ultra-keen price point, but most of these technicalities won’t bother the target audience at that great deal of a price tag.
That’s not to say that the MacBook Neo is perfect—otherwise why would the MacBook Air and Pro exist? For not a whole lot of extra outlay you can make the MacBook Neo an even better product and part of your digital lifestyle with these accessories. Here we list some of our favorite Mac accessories that we think every MacBook Neo owner should purchase or at least put on their wish list.
MacBook Neo limitations and solutions
Here are some of the limitations of the MacBook Neo that you can solve with the accessories in this guide. 
Slow 20W charger: Buy a faster charger
Only two USB-C ports: Buy a USB-C hub
One slow 480Mbps port: Buy a USB-C hub
Single external display support: Buy a DisplayLink dock
Small screen for desk use: Buy an external screen

				
					

				
			
Satechi




Essential MacBook Neo accessory 1: A charger
Apple ships the MacBook Neo with a 20-watt (20W) Power Adapter (unless you’re in the U.K. or E.U., where–tough luck–you’ll get just a charging cable and no actual charger). At just 20W, it’s a pretty low-powered adapter to be honest. In fact, it’s now hard to find a charger rated that low, with 30W or 45W increasingly the minimum output.
If you’re in a hurry for power, you’ll want something more capable than Apple’s puny 20W adapter. While Apple doesn’t list fast charging in the Neo’s tech specs, in our own Neo charging tests we found it does charge faster when paired with a more powerful charger.
Charging speed is largely determined by power output. The more watts available, the faster a device can charge—up to its maximum supported input. For example, you can plug a 140W charger into an iPhone, but it won’t charge any faster than it would with a 35W adapter as the Neo’s max input is 30W. A 30W charger will be faster than the 20W but a little more powerful supply will get through any latency. We recommend at least a 35W charger. Better still, buy a much more powerful charger with multiple ports so you can charge more than just your Neo with it.
We’ve chosen two alternative chargers to consider: a compact 45W single-port model and a 65W multiport charger. For more options, see our roundup of the best USB-C chargers for MacBook for even more choice.

The Apple 20W charger is just a plain white brick with non-foldable plug pins. It measures 1.63 x 1.67 x 1.06 inches (41 x 42 x 27mm). The Belkin BoostCharge Compact is smaller at 1.32 x 1.32 x 1.36 inches (33.5 x 33.5 x 34.5mm), and features foldable plugs (U.S. and U.K.). The Anker 45W Nano Charger features even more flexible 180-degree dual foldable plug pins that are designed to adapt to any outlet angle while keeping the screen clearly visible and/or USB-C port easy to locate.
It’s smarter too. It has a front display that gives you real-time updates on power, temperature, and charging modes. The Anker Nano is smaller than the Apple charger but at 1.34 x 1.38 x 1.57 inches (34 x 35 x 40mm) a little larger than the Belkin. The Ugreen Nexode is a multiport wall charger available in 65W (2 ports) or 100W (3 ports) models, each with the integrated 2.5-foot cable.

							
		
Essential MacBook Neo accessory 2: More ports
The MacBook Neo has just two USB-C ports on one side. You’ll need one for your charging cable (included in the box), leaving just one port spare to connect other devices such as storage thumb drives, external displays, card readers, and so on.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




One of the Neo’s two USB-C ports is limited to a 480Mbps data transfer rate—that’s up to 250 times slower than the Thunderbolt 5 port on a MacBook Pro—that will really bore the pants off you during a long backup to an external storage device. Use the slow one for your charging cable, and save the other much faster 10Gbps USB-C to connect a hub that boasts many more types of ports to make your Neo more like a proper desktop workstation.
We like the Satechi OnTheGo Multiport Adapter reviewed below because it comes in all the Neo colors as does the Satechi Snap Hub. However, there are many more to choose from, adding between 4 and 12 extra ports, including USB-C and USB-A ports, card readers, Ethernet, HDMI, and more. There’s sure to be the perfect one for you and your MacBook Neo. See our reviews of all the best USB-C hubs and adapters for MacBooks. Satechi’s USB-C Snap Hub might be the best hub for most MacBook Neo owners, combining a perfectly color-matched, flush-fitting design with the essential ports the Neo lacks at an affordable price. Available in Citrus, Blush, Indigo, and Silver, it looks like a natural extension of the laptop while adding charging, USB expansion, HDMI, and SD card support in a compact, cable-free design.
It’s engineered specifically for MacBook Neo’s asymmetric USB-C port design, and measures 3.95 x 1.43 x 0.39 inches (100 x 29 x 10mm) with a marginal weight of 1.13oz (32g).
It does take up both of the Neo’s adjacent USB-C ports but replaces these and adds much more—offering two USB-C ports (one for 45W power delivery, and one for 5Gbps data), one legacy USB-A port, HDMI, and both SD and MicroSD card readers. 
While the Neo supports just one external display, this is ably handled by the HMI port that supports up to a $k display at a 60Hz refresh rate. If you desire more than one display, you’ll need a DisplayLink dock: see lower down for this solution.

Satechi has really gone into bat for MacBook Neo users. Not only does it sell the Neo-matching USB-C Snap Hub reviewed above, it has gone all Citrus, Blush, Indigo, and Silver on its OnTheGo Multiport Adapter.
Connect this cute hub to the spare USB-C port—make sure it’s the fast 10Gbps one near the end of the Neo’s side—and you instantly get access to a range of ports denied to non-hub users. Many of these you don’t get even with the top-end MacBook Pro. It’s magnetic so can clamp to metal objects and comes with a magnetic adhesive ring that you can stick to the front of your Neo.
There are two versions: a 5-in-1 that comes in Neo colors and a 7-in-1 that’s redulation black.
The OnTheGo Multiport Adapter is a portable pocket-sized hockey puck shape (65mm diameter) with a coiled braided USB-C cable and either five or seven varied ports. The 5-in-1 features two USB-C ports (one ready to passthrough up to 60W of power to the Neo, although it will use only 30W of that), one legacy USB-A port, an SD card reader, and HDMI 2.0 for connecting an external display (up to 4K/60Hz).
If you need Gigabit Ethernet to access a stable, fast wired network, you’ll need to forego the Neo colors for the black-only 7-in-1 model. That model also comes with a MicroSD card reader alomgside the SD reader, plus a second USB-A port, although it does lack the USB-C data port.
What might interest Neo owners are the card readers that are ideal for adding cheap, portable storage. You can pick up a 256GB microSD card for $50, 512GB for $100, and 1TB for around $250, although storage prices can be very volatile.
Read our full Satechi OnTheGo Multiport Adapter review.

							
		
Essential MacBook Neo accessory 3: A desk stand
A laptop is a far more flexible computer than one always tethered to your desk, but that portability and ability to work just about anywhere comes with a hidden price: sore shoulders and back. Ergonomics—the study of people in their working environment—proves that being hunched over a laptop screen and keyboard takes a toll on your body; particularly musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) such as carpal tunnel syndrome, back pain, and tendonitis caused by repetitive strain and awkward postures.
One solution is to raise the laptop to a better height and angle so that your neck and shoulders are relieved from those dangers, and that is best sorted by using a laptop stand with your MacBook Neo. For more adjustable options go to our reviews of the best MacBook stands.

title: With iOS 27.3, the Siri AI floodgates are about to open
content:
Macworld





With the new OS 27.3 betas (iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS), Apple is finally making good on one of those old Apple Intelligence features it first promised back in 2024.
When Apple announced Apple Intelligence and all its fancy new features, one of the most important aspects was personal context, its ability to perform actions and access data across all your apps. A massive expansion of “App Intents,” the feature would allow developers to make their apps work with Siri by making some of the content or data accessible and allow users to perform actions in those apps with natural language.
According to a post on Apple’s developer site, Siri AI is finally going to realize this vision with the 27.3 beta releases:
Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order. For complex requests, we’re also introducing skills to let you teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience. And Siri AI can now surface any entity in the Spotlight semantic index, not just the ones that fit an existing schema.
The new beta previews allow developers to integrate their apps into Siri AI, allowing users to access data and perform actions. Developers can build custom actions for users, and incorporate skills that teach Siri how to combine several actions into a single request
The blog post calls this a “sneak peek” and a “first look,” so it’s not clear yet when regular users will get this experience. Developers can currently build apps using these Intents and Skills and test them with Xcode or with internal TestFlight versions, but they can’t publish apps that use these features to the App Store or test them with external TestFlight users yet.
It’s likely that app developers will be able to publish their Siri AI enabled apps with the OS 27.3 updates are released to the general public (we expect in late November or early December), but that depends on developer feedback and testing. Still, this is the first time developers have actually had real access to integrate their apps with the new Siri, and once released and widespread, it can change the way we use our iPhones, iPads, and Macs forever.

Many of us are quite used to carrying around a handy power bank to top up our iPhone batteries during a long day away from a power socket, but these pocketable battery packs are usually not powerful enough to keep an unplugged and energy-hungry MacBook going all day.
We’ve rounded up the best portable laptop power banks with battery capacities high enough to recharge a fading Apple MacBook if you won’t be able to plug it into an electrical outlet for some time.
Despite new laptops boasting improved battery life duration, it’s easy for your trusty MacBook to lose power after a day of intense meetings and PowerPoint presentations. No one wants to see the Mac’s “Your battery is running low” warning, especially when halfway through watching a downloaded Netflix series on a long-haul flight.
We looked at seven main factors for recommending laptop power banks: battery capacity, charging speed, total power output, power input, USB ports, portability and safety. For more details on each see below this list of the best MacBook power banks.
Power vs portability
As a rule, the higher the battery capacity, the larger and heavier the power bank. We have included size and weight so you can determine if each power bank suits your traveling needs. Some laptop power banks are built to last in the great outdoors so will feature more rugged IP-rated shells; read on for our reviews below.
There are much smaller, lighter and more portable power banks for phones—check out our recommendations of the best power banks for iPhone. You could use some of these to recharge a laptop but we recommend the power banks tested and reviewed here for the best results when powering up a laptop.
There are some giant power banks, usually called portable power stations, that can keep a family going all weekend, but they are way too large to carry with you on your travels. We have tested the most MacBook-friendly models in our roundup of the best portable power stations.
Macworld Test Score
We test each power bank’s real-world charging prowess by recharging a spent 14-inch MacBook Pro from 0% to 100% (or as far as it gets) and then repeat, adding the two percentages together to create a comparable Test Score.
Which power bank is best for your MacBook in 2026?
We have indicated which models of MacBook we think each power bank is best suited to, but that doesn’t mean you can’t pair any with different MacBooks. The 16-inch MacBook Pro can be fast-charged at 140W so owners of that model should look for a PD 3.1 power bank. But even a 13-inch MacBook Air or MacBook Neo will work well with the higher-capacity power banks. They might not charge any faster, but they will be recharged more times if you pick a high-capacity battery pack.

The Anker Prime 26K Power Bank (300W) is one of the most powerful laptop power banks that you can match with your MacBook. It is a great fit with the top-end 16-inch MacBook Pro, which has a battery rated at around the same watt hours (99.6WH) as this power bank (99.75Wh).

Anker claims that you can fast-charge that top-end MacBook Pro up to 50% in 27 minutes. In our tests, we charged a 14-inch M2 MacBook Pro to full power with enough left over to power it back to 25% on the second recharge.
You can recharge the power bank itself to 50% in under 15 minutes using the two USB-C ports at the same time at an impressive 250W.
This is a sophisticated power bank with some tricks of its own. It can be controlled by an app, which gives real-time charging stats (Remaining Charging Time and Input and Output power indicators) and can be optimized to help extend the battery life of the devices being charged as well as its own. You can even use the app’s Find Device feature to activate a sound alert from the power bank when you need to locate it.
Anker also sells a 27K Prime Power Bank, available in either black or gold colors. We prefer the 26K model as it’s a little smaller, performed better in our tests, and out guns the 27K model in total output (300W vs 250W) and input (250W vs 170W).

The very affordable Sharge HyperTower 170 Power Bank scored impressively in our MacBook recharging tests (128%) despite its 25K (90Wh) battery capacity being a little lower than seen in some others.
The 170W total power output is also lower than some (we’ve tested power banks with as much as 300W total output) but still offers a lot. Even with all three outputs in use it supports 100W+30W+20W+15W or 65W+65W+20W+15W, so can handle a two-laptop setup.
100W input is fine if you’re not in the biggest hurry to recharge the power bank—we’ve all been there—and it should be fully recharged in around 80 minutes. If power bank input is important to you, check out the Anker Prime 26K Power Bank reviewed above.
Especially useful are the two integrated USB-C cables (each 100W), one of which doubles up as a carry handle. The USB-C port is also 100W capable.

Power bank battery capacity
The larger the laptop power bank’s capacity the more charges it will be able to give your MacBook. While nearly all laptop power banks give their battery capacity in milliamp hours (mAh) it’s more instructional to know the battery capacity in watt hours (Wh) as Wh provides a more accurate estimation of a battery’s energy capacity for devices with varying power requirements.
A 13-inch MacBook Air has a battery capacity of around 50Wh; a MacBook Neo’s is smaller at 36.5Wh. The 16-inch MacBook Pro’s battery is rated at nearly twice that—just under 100Wh. To find out the Wh rating of your MacBook, check our our list of all the MacBook battery capacities.
In theory, a 100Wh power bank could recharge the smaller laptop twice and the larger one once. While it’s not quite that simple—due to issues such as the laptop using some power during charging and environmental conditions such as temperature—you will certainly get more charge from a power bank with a higher Wh rating.
Watt hours is also the measure used by airlines to determine whether you can carry the power bank onto a plane with you: see below our list of the best MacBook power banks for national and international in-flight battery regulations. 
Battery to laptop charging speed
The speed at which a power bank can charge your laptop is important, especially if you are charging the MacBook while using it.
Like any USB-C charger, look for the wattage at which the power bank can output power. A small laptop (especially the Neo) requires perhaps as little as 40W to keep it powered up. A larger MacBook might require 65W or 100W. A 16-inch MacBook Pro can be fast-charged at 140W.
In technical terms, chargers and power banks have a USB PD (Power Delivery) rating. PD 3.0 has a maximum power output of 100W. PD 3.1 (useful for the 16-inch MacBook Pro) can output at 140W. The PD rating is assigned to each USB port (see below).
That top-end MacBook can be charged at 100W, but it will take longer to charge. If you use a much lower wattage charger, or power bank, your MacBook battery might not fill up as fast because the laptop battery is being used by your applications.
As such we haven’t looked at any laptop power bank rated at under 65W and make recommendations for each power bank we have tested as to which MacBook model it is best suited for.
It is fine to use a 140W PD 3.1 charger or power bank on a smaller laptop—nothing untoward will happen as the power output is regulated by the laptop being powered. Indeed, you can safely charge your AirPods case with a 140W charger even though it won’t take more than 5W.
Total power output
A power bank with multiple ports will also have a maximum total output, which is how much power all the ports can give out together at one time when each is connected to a different device.
A power bank might have two ports each rated at 100W, but if the total power output is 100W then that power will be shared between the ports. Look for a total power output that means the power bank can handle charging multiple devices at the same time at full speed.
Power input
Power Input is the wattage at which the power bank itself can be charged via a USB-C charger. Again, the more watts, the faster the charge up to the power bank’s full capacity.
USB ports
A power bank needs at least one USB port to carry the power from itself to the device being charged. USB ports today come in two basic varieties: old-school rectangular USB-A and modern reversible USB-C.
You will get the fastest charge using USB-C at the power bank end. At the MacBook end, the USB-C end of the cable will connect with the MacBook’s Thunderbolt port, which is identical to USB-C in looks and basic operation. Thunderbolt is backward compatible with USB-C.
Look for power banks with multiple USB ports so you can charge more than one device at a time: more than one laptop, or a laptop plus a phone or two, or your AirPods case and Apple Watch. A USB-A port might be useful if you need to power-up a device whose charger uses the older standard; for example, a Fitbit.
Some power banks include a DC port, which is handy for devices such as high-end camera rigs that don’t work with USB-C.
Power bank safety
Batteries can present a fire risk in certain circumstances, such as rapid overheating (a process called thermal runaway), overcharging and exposure to high temperatures. As such we recommend only power banks from trusted, premium manufacturers with a long record of producing safe, high-quality products. You will find cheaper power banks, but we believe that the safety of the device you are charging, your home or office, plus your bag if carrying it around with you, are paramount.
If you want to take your power bank on a plane, there are also regulations to abide by—or you’ll be leaving it at the Security Desk. See below the chart of our favorite laptop power banks for international airline rules on permitted power banks and batteries.
Which spare batteries and power banks can you take on a plane?
When damaged, short-circuited or overheated, batteries can catch fire and explode, so there are regulations in place to ensure safety onboard commercial aircraft.
If you are lucky you’ll find a charging point at the airport, but we know these are usually already taken. Many plane seats also have a USB port, but it’s often old-school USB-A where most chargers these days use the more modern, powerful and reversible USB-C connector.
You’d be wise to carry your own USB-C wall charger, which you can use if your plane seat includes a regular AC power socket. Remember that you might need a travel adapter depending on the nationality of the airline.
Most U.S. flight regulations allow for lithium-ion batteries up to 160Wh, if permitted by the individual airlines, but international airlines such as in Europe don’t allow you to use the power bank in flight (either to charge a devices or be charged itself).
U.S. TSA and FAA battery and power bank regulations
The U.S. Transportation Security Administration (TSA) states that any “spare (uninstalled) lithium ion and lithium metal batteries, including power banks and cell phone battery charging cases, must be carried in carry-on baggage only”.
Both TSA and the Federal Aviation Administration (FFA) state that “with airline approval”, passengers may also carry up to two spare larger lithium-ion batteries (101–160Wh).
TSA requirements apply to both air carriers and airports, and the FAA requirements only apply to commercial airlines.
U.K. Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) battery and power bank regulations
Up to two “spare batteries for portable electronic devices containing lithium-ion batteries exceeding a Watt-hour rating of 100Wh but not exceeding 160Wh when carried for personal use are allowed for carry-on baggage and on one’s person. They are not permitted in checked (hold) baggage.”
Airlines do not allow the power bank to be used during flight or be charged itself when in the air.
European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) battery and power bank regulations
The European Union regulations are stricter: “If the Wh is higher than 100 but not higher than 160, you will need an approval from the operator to carry the item”.
EASA also states that “power banks should not be connected or providing power to a device while on board the aircraft”. So you can carry the power bank with you but not actually recharge your phone or laptop while on the plane.
How to find a battery’s Watt Hour (Wh) rating
Manufacturers are required to mark lithium-ion batteries with the watt-hour rating, but it’s often not clearly indicated on the packaging or on the power bank itself—look for some tiny writing on one side of the battery pack and you’ll eventually find the Wh rating. Don’t worry, we’ve done that for you in our recommendations below. You can calculate the number of watt-hours your battery provides if you know the battery’s nominal voltage (V) and capacity in ampere-hours (Ah), by using this calculation: Ah x V = Wh.
If you know only the battery’s milliampere hours (mAh), divide that number by 1,000 to get the ampere-hours (Ah). For example, 1200mAh divided by 1,000 = 1.2Ah. Then multiply that number by the power bank’s voltage.

title: How to handle a water spill on your Mac before the damage gets worse
content:
A liquid spill can damage your Mac long after the surface dries, making a quick response essential to avoiding an expensive repair. Here's how to limit the damage and give your Mac the best chance of recovery.

If you spill water on your Mac
If you spill water on your Mac, shut it down, disconnect power, and blot away visible moisture before checking how far the liquid spread. Water can seep through the keyboard, ports, and gaps in the enclosure, reaching sensitive components even when the outside looks dry.
A few drops on the aluminum enclosure are different from a full cup of coffee spilling across the keyboard. The amount of liquid, where it enters, and what it contains all affect the risk of damage.
Coffee, soda, and other drinks can also leave behind residue that causes problems long after the liquid evaporates. Liquid damage isn't always obvious, and a Mac that continues working after a spill isn't necessarily safe to use.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4 guide: Price, features, battery life and updates
content:
Macworld





In September 2026 Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, with both models focusing much more heavily on health monitoring, Apple Intelligence and battery efficiency than on physical redesigns. Series 12 remains Apple’s mainstream premium smartwatch, while Ultra 4 continues as the larger, tougher model aimed at endurance sports, outdoor activities and diving. Both Apple Watches went on sale on September 18.
The biggest upgrade shared by both watches is Apple’s all-new Health Sensing System, which combines redesigned optical and electrical heart sensors with larger, more power-efficient green LEDs. Apple says it provides the most accurate heart-rate sensing of any wearable it tested. Background heart-rate readings are now taken every five seconds, while HRV can be measured as often as every five minutes – 60 times and 24 times more frequently respectively than on Series 11.
That additional data powers another major addition: Readiness, which gives users a 0–10 score based on recent activity, sleep, vitals and recovery data, and updates during the day. Both watches also use Apple’s new S11 chip, which enables Siri AI and a collection of Audio Intelligence features including Sound Recognition, faster Shazam, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are available to test in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta, released on November 3, 2026. Both initially support English only.
The most dramatic hardware improvement is reserved for the Ultra 4: Apple has increased its normal-use battery-life rating from 42 hours to 50 hours, Low Power Mode from 72 to 84 hours, and introduced workout modes capable of tracking for up to 45 hours. Series 12 remains rated at 24 hours, although our testing found inconsistent battery life and charging performance, while the aluminium Series 12 gains tougher Ceramic Shield 2 and Apple has brought back a premium ceramic Apple Watch for the first time in years.
The five biggest Apple Watch upgrades for 2026
New Health Sensing System with substantially more frequent heart-rate and HRV monitoring.
Readiness score for daily recovery and training guidance. 
S11 chip, Siri AI and Audio Intelligence, including Siri Recap and Live Rewind, now in watchOS 27.3 developer-beta testing.
Much longer Ultra 4 battery life, rising from 42 to 50 hours, with up to 45 hours of extended workout tracking.
New materials and durability, including Ceramic Shield 2 on aluminium Series 12 and the return of ceramic Series 12 models.
The rumours were broadly right that this wouldn’t be a major redesign, and also correctly predicted the emphasis on health, Siri AI and ceramic materials. However, rumours of Touch ID have not materialised, there is still no blood-glucose sensor, and the Series 12 hasn’t gained longer quoted battery life despite speculation about a larger battery. Starting prices are unchanged, although the 46mm Series 12 costs more.

				
					

				
			
Your watch knows how you are feeling. Do you? 

Apple




Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4: Specs compared


FeatureApple Watch Series 12Apple Watch Ultra 4

Health Sensing SystemNew optical/electrical sensorsSame new system
Background heart rateEvery 5 secondsEvery 5 seconds
HRVAs often as every 5 minutesAs often as every 5 minutes
Readiness scoreYesYes, with training data
ProcessorS11S11
Siri AIYes (beta; language and regional restrictions apply)Yes (beta; language and regional restrictions apply)
Audio IntelligenceSupported; Live Rewind and Siri Recap available in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta, initially in English.Supported; Live Rewind and Siri Recap available in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta, initially in English.
Display42mm/46mm, up to 2,000 nits49mm, up to 3,000 nits
BatteryUp to 24 hours; 38 hours Low PowerUp to 50 hours; 84 hours Low Power
SatelliteNo direct satellite communicationsMessages, Emergency SOS and Find My via satellite

 






Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 release date and availability
Apple announced the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 on September 9, 2026. Both models went on sale on September 18 and are available from Apple, authorized retailers and participating carriers.
watchOS 27 was released on September 14 for compatible existing Apple Watches.
Both watches are available now, including in the U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada and more than 50 other countries and regions.
You can buy them directly from Apple through Apple.com, the Apple Store app and Apple retail stores. They are also available through Apple-authorised retailers and, in the case of cellular models, participating mobile networks.
$389.99 at  Amazon										 | 
																$389.99 at  Walmart										 | 
																$399 at  Apple United States						
					
$699.99 at  Amazon										 | 
																$774 at  Walmart										 | 
																$799 at  Apple United States						
					
Buy Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 at Apple U.S. 
Buy Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 at Apple U.K. 


							


Apple Watch Series 12 design

				
					

				
			
The Apple Watch Series 12 in bronze.

David Price / Foundry




The Series 12 does not represent a major external redesign, as the pre-launch rumours suggested. It retains Apple’s familiar rounded-square design and comes in 42mm and 46mm sizes.
Interestingly, the aluminium and titanium cases are fractionally wider than Series 11. The 46mm model measures 46 x 40 x 9.7mm, compared with 46 x 39 x 9.7mm for Series 11. The 42mm version measures 42 x 37 x 9.7mm, compared with 42 x 36 x 9.7mm previously. The screen resolutions remain 416×496 pixels and 374×446 pixels respectively.
Apple continues to offer aluminium and titanium models, but ceramic has returned as a premium case option. Ceramic models are fractionally larger and thicker, measuring 43mm or 47mm tall and 9.85mm thick.
The finishes are:
Aluminium: Dark Bronze, Light Gold, Black and Space Grey
Titanium: Radiant Gold and Natural
Ceramic: Pearl White and Night Blue
The ceramic options confirm one of the more interesting pre-launch rumours, although Apple opted for Night Blue rather than the dark grey that had also been indicated.
The Series 12 display remains a wide-angle LTPO3 Always-On Retina OLED with up to 2,000 nits brightness. Aluminium models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the Ion-X glass used on Series 11. Titanium and ceramic versions use sapphire crystal.


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 4 design

				
					

				
			
The rugged Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Apple




The Ultra 4 changes even less externally. It remains a 49mm Grade 5 titanium watch, measuring exactly 49 x 44 x 12mm, with the same 422×514-pixel display and 1,245 sq mm display area as Ultra 3.
It comes in the familiar Natural Titanium and Black Titanium finishes and retains its flat sapphire crystal display, raised protective case edges, prominent Digital Crown and orange-accented Action button.
The Ultra 4 is slightly heavier, however: 63.0g in Natural and 63.1g in Black, compared with 61.6g and 61.8g respectively for Ultra 3.
The display remains a wide-angle LTPO3 Always-On Retina display capable of 3,000 nits, so there is no headline screen-brightness upgrade.
Apple hasn’t introduced the rumoured Touch ID fingerprint sensor on the 2026 Apple Watch models. 


						

							


What about the buttons and controls?

				
					

				
			
The side button.

Apple




The physical control layout is essentially unchanged.
Series 12 has:
Digital Crown with haptic feedback
Side button
Strap-release buttons
Ultra 4 adds the familiar:
Customisable Action button
Larger protected Digital Crown
Side button
The Action button can start workouts, mark segments, move to the next interval, activate the torch and perform other user-selected actions.
There is, however, a new single-tap finger-and-thumb gesture in addition to Double Tap and Wrist Flick, providing another way to interact without touching the display.


						

							


Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 health features
The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 share the same new Health Sensing System and Readiness features. Paying more for the Ultra doesn’t get you more advanced core health sensors.

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




More frequent heart-rate and HRV tracking
Both watches have redesigned optical and electrical heart sensors, including larger, more power-efficient green LEDs. Background heart-rate readings are taken every five seconds, while heart rate variability (HRV) can be measured as often as every five minutes. These more frequent measurements provide a fuller picture of your activity and recovery throughout the day.
HRV measures variation in the time between heartbeats. The watches distinguish between Recovery HRV, which helps assess shorter-term stress and recovery, and overall HRV, which provides insight into longer-term health trends. Recovery HRV is also included in overnight Vitals, where it is compared with your personal baseline. A new daytime Vitals view shows heart rate and HRV, helping you spot changes outside your usual ranges.
Readiness: Should you push harder or take it easy?
Readiness combines recent activity, training load, daytime and overnight vitals, and sleep data into a score from 0 to 10. It provides one of four recommendations:
Recover: 0–1
Pace Yourself: 2–4
Ready: 5–7
Go For It: 8–10
The score updates throughout the day as you exercise, rest or take a nap. Open the Readiness app to see how activity, vitals and sleep are influencing it.
You’ll need to set up Activity, Sleep and overnight Vitals, enter your health details, and wear the watch to bed for at least seven nights before receiving a score. Readiness is a wellness guide: it doesn’t account for every medical condition or medication and shouldn’t be your sole basis for deciding whether it is safe to exercise.
Returning health features
Both watches retain ECG, high and low heart-rate notifications, irregular-rhythm notifications, blood oxygen tracking, sleep stages, sleep score, sleep apnea notifications and temperature-based Cycle Tracking. These features are also available on earlier compatible Apple Watches, although availability varies by model and region.
Hypertension notifications look for patterns associated with chronic high blood pressure over 30-day periods; they don’t provide a blood-pressure reading. The feature also supports earlier compatible models, and availability on Series 12 and Ultra 4 remains subject to regulatory clearance in some regions.
Do the new sensors affect battery life?
In Macwelt’s comparison of the Series 12 and Series 11, Halyna Kubiv recorded more background activity on the newer watch but lower energy consumption during the period after a hike.
That comparison covered a single day, and the watches differed in iPhone pairing and display use. It suggests the additional monitoring can be efficient, but doesn’t prove it has no effect on battery life.


						

							


Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 processor: What processor do they use?
Both watches use Apple’s new S11 chip, replacing the S10 used by Series 11 and Ultra 3.
Apple’s specifications list:
64-bit dual-core processor
4-core Neural Engine
64GB storage
Secure hardware for Audio Intelligence processing
The S10 also had a 64-bit dual-core CPU, four-core Neural Engine and 64GB of storage, so the headline specifications alone don’t reveal how much faster S11 actually is. Apple calls it its “most powerful wearable chip”, but notably hasn’t provided a percentage CPU or GPU performance improvement over S10, and its technical specifications don’t list a separate GPU core count.
That means the more important S11 improvements appear to be what the chip enables rather than raw benchmark performance.
It works with the new Health Sensing System, supports Siri AI and powers the new Audio Intelligence functionality. Apple has also emphasised efficiency, particularly in relation to higher-frequency sensor readings and Ultra 4’s improved battery life.
The new Audio Intelligence system includes a Secure Exclave, a hardware-isolated area of the S11 that processes audio separately and deletes raw audio immediately after processing.


						

							


2026 Apple Watch connectivity

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Connectivity changes are modest. Cellular Series 12 and Ultra 4 models support 5G RedCap and LTE, as did their predecessors, with no newly branded Apple-designed modem.
Both watches also support Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n) on 2.4GHz and 5GHz, Bluetooth 5.3, and Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip. Wi-Fi 4 may sound dated, but Apple Watch relies mainly on Bluetooth and has relatively low data requirements.
Satellite connectivity
Satellite communications remain a major distinction between the Series and Ultra families.
Apple Watch Series 12 doesn’t have built-in satellite connectivity.
Ultra 4 does, supporting Emergency SOS via satellite and Find My location sharing via satellite when cellular and Wi-Fi aren’t available. 
This is in addition to Messages via Satellite, which arrived in September 2025 with the Apple Watch Ultra 3. That feature lets you send and receive personal messages when your watch has no cellular or Wi-Fi coverage. However, Messages via satellite is available only in the US, Canada, Mexico and Japan. The new Emergency SOS via satellite is available in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Australia, New Zealand, various European countries, Japan and Mexico. No cellular plan is required for Emergency SOS via satellite.
This is broadly what had been expected before launch: Satellite remains primarily an Ultra feature rather than migrating to the regular Series watch.


						

							


2026 Apple Watch battery and charging: What’s new?

				
					

				
			
Charging the Apple Watch. 

Apple




Apple Watch Series 12
Apple rates Series 12 for:
Up to 24 hours normal use
Up to 38 hours in Low Power Mode
Up to 10 hours of outdoor workout tracking
Those first two figures are unchanged from Series 11, so despite rumours that Apple was working on a larger battery, there is no increase in Apple’s quoted everyday battery life.
Apple claims improved endurance from a short charge.
Apple quotes the following charging figures for Series 12:
80 percent in around 30 minutes
Up to 12 hours of use from a 15-minute charge
Up to 10 hours of sleep tracking from five minutes of charging
Apple also rated Series 11 for an 80 percent charge in around 30 minutes, and up to eight hours of normal use from a 15-minute charge.
In our Apple Watch Series 12 review, we recorded 51 and 40 hours of battery life across two runs – an average of 45.5 hours, compared with 47.5 hours for Series 11. Charging also varied: our watch reached 58% and 72% after 30 minutes in separate tests, falling short of Apple’s claimed 80%. These results show that the Series 12 can comfortably exceed Apple’s 24-hour rating, but they don’t demonstrate a consistent improvement over Series 11. Actual battery life depends on usage.
A separate investigation by Macwelt’s Halyna Kubiv compared Series 11 and Series 12 during a seven-hour hike and subsequent everyday use. After the workout, Series 12 recorded more background activity but consumed less energy during the measured period. However, this was a one-day comparison with different conditions: Series 11 was actively paired with an iPhone and handling notifications, while Series 12 was not, and display use differed. 
Apple Watch Ultra 4
Battery life is one of Ultra 4’s biggest upgrades.
Apple rates it for:
50 hours normal use, up from 42 hours
84 hours Low Power Mode, up from 72 hours
18 hours standard outdoor workout tracking
25 hours Extended Workout
45 hours Max Extended Workout
Apple says the Extended Workout figure represents a 25 percent increase over the previous generation.
Apple says Ultra 4 can reach 80 percent in around 45 minutes, but 15 minutes of charging now provides up to 18 hours of use, versus 12 hours on Ultra 3.
Apple also credits more efficient workout algorithms with helping deliver the longer endurance.
Apple Watch charging
Both models use Apple’s magnetic fast-charging system with the Apple Watch Magnetic Fast Charger to USB-C Cable.
There is no change to the basic magnetic charging system this year.


						

							


Siri AI: Availability and requirements
Siri AI remains in beta, with availability depending on your language and region. The watchOS 27.2 update, released on October 26, adds French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish alongside English. Apple says Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish and Vietnamese will follow by the end of 2026.
Siri AI requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled device set to a supported language. It is currently unavailable on Apple Watch in the European Union and is not available to users under 13.


						

							


What is Audio Intelligence? 
Audio Intelligence is Apple’s collection of sound-based AI features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. These include recognizing important sounds, identifying music, displaying recently spoken words and summarizing conversations.
Sound Recognition and automatic Music Recognition with Shazam are already available. Live Rewind and Siri Recap entered developer-beta testing with watchOS 27.3 on November 3, 2026, so are likely to arrive with the full version of watchOS 27.3 later in 2026.
These two features require a supported iPhone 16 or newer, excluding iPhone 16e, with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI enabled. They initially support English only, are restricted to users aged 18 or older, and are unavailable in China and initially in the European Union. Sound Recognition and automatic Music Recognition support a wider range of iPhones and do not share these restrictions.


						

							






Sound RecognitionAlerts you to sounds such as alarms and doorbellsAvailable now
Automatic Music RecognitionIdentifies background music in the Smart StackAvailable now
Live RewindDisplays the previous 15 seconds of speech as textAvailable in watchOS 27.3 developer beta
Siri RecapGenerates summaries of conversationsAvailable in watchOS 27.3 developer beta

 



Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 price
Apple has kept its entry prices unchanged in both the U.S. and U.K. – contrary to pre-event speculation that the Series 12 could increase in price.


Model2026 pricePrevious generation

Series 12 – U.S.42mm $399 / 46mm $449Series 11: 42mm $399 / 46mm $429
Series 12 – U.K.42mm £369 / 46mm £419Series 11: 42mm £369 / 46mm £399
Ultra 4 – U.S.From $799Ultra 3: $799
Ultra 4 – U.K.From £749Ultra 3: £749

 



Series 12 pricing varies considerably depending on case material. Aluminium is the entry-level option, while titanium costs more and the newly revived ceramic models occupy the premium end of the range.
Starting prices are unchanged, but the larger Series 12 costs more. The 46mm aluminum model starts at $449/£419 with GPS or $549/£519 with cellular—an increase of $20/£20 over the equivalent Series 11 models.
Should you buy Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Apple Watch Series 12 is the best choice for most people. It offers essentially all of Apple’s important new features – including the new Health Sensing System, Readiness, frequent HRV measurements, Siri AI and Audio Intelligence – in a considerably smaller and cheaper watch. Live Rewind and Siri Recap currently require the watchOS 27.3 developer beta.
However, our Series 12 review found inconsistent battery life and charging, along with occasional sluggishness. These observations may not reflect an established problem affecting every watch, but they temper our recommendation, particularly for owners of recent models considering an upgrade.
The strongest reason to choose Ultra 4 is battery life. Its increase in Apple’s rated battery life from 42 to 50 hours makes it much more practical for people who regularly spend more than a day away from a charger, while the new 25- and 45-hour extended workout modes make it substantially more appealing to runners, hikers, cyclists and endurance athletes.
Ultra 4 is also the better choice for outdoor adventurers because of its brighter 3,000-nit display, dual-frequency GPS, rugged titanium construction, Action button, 100m water resistance, recreational diving support and satellite communications. Series 12 is the better everyday watch: lighter, less bulky, available in two sizes and substantially cheaper.

title: Everything New in the iOS 27.3 Beta
content:
Apple today started testing iOS 27.3, the biggest update to iOS 27 since it launched in September. iOS 27.3 includes some features Apple showed off earlier this year, and it adds all-new capabilities.

Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos.


Safari

Safari has a Vertical Tabs layout option that can be activated in Safari settings, along with an Adaptive Dark Mode for websites that don't have a dark mode design option.


Siri AI

Siri AI can do more in and across apps, with Apple adding a long list of new actions.


In Mail, ‌Siri‌ can unsubscribe you from mailing lists and undo recently sent messages. In Weather, ‌Siri‌ can add locations to your weather list, or control weather notifications. In Safari, ‌Siri‌ can clear browsing history, manage tabs and windows, save articles to a Reading List, and close duplicate tabs. In Files, ‌Siri‌ can organize content, delete files you haven't accessed for a set period of time, and more.

Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. You can find out what's new by asking ‌Siri‌ what it can do in each app.

integrate their app with ‌Siri‌ AI.

Any app can now bring its content and actions directly into ‌Siri‌ AI using App Intents. ‌Siri‌ AI can complete any custom actions developers implement, and there are skills available for teaching ‌Siri‌ AI to combine several actions into a single experience.

New Health App

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. It has new Insights and Longevity tabs that show more information about your health and fitness metrics.


The Insights tab includes your most recent health data, like Activity Rings, heart rate, sleep score, and vitals. Apple Intelligence will use that information to offer Personal Guidance. The Health app will be able to make suggestions based on your goals and what kinds of activities you do.

The Health app's Longevity tab looks at health data over time. It assesses you across seven categories: heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing, and nutrition. It also has a Health Age feature that uses info like resting heart rate, VO2 max, HRV, sleep, and biomarkers from blood work to calculate how your health metrics compare to your actual age. Health Age relies on health data collected from the Apple Watch, plus it incorporates fitness assessments you can take at home with tracking via the iPhone's camera.

iPhone Duo Reachability

Reachability is now available on the iPhone Duo. You can swipe left from the left edge or right from the right edge of the device's outer display to bring content closer to where your thumb is for one-handed use.



Reachability can be turned on in the Settings app by going to Accessibility, selecting Touch, and toggling on the option.

iPhone Duo Keyboard

The keyboard on the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s front display has been tweaked. The emoji and number keys have been swapped, as have the microphone and return keys. 


Keys are slightly taller and thinner, the space bar is wider, and the letters on each key are smaller and not as bold. 

StandBy

Apple is making the StandBy features introduced with the ‌iPhone Duo‌ available on all iPhone models that can run ‌iOS 27‌. There are updated versions of the Analog and Digital Clock faces with more customization options for color and complications, an updated ‌Photos‌ face, new Calendar and Weather faces, and the option to create multiple versions of each face type and swipe between them.

Live Rewind and Siri Recap

Live Rewind and Siri Recap are available in watchOS 27.3, but iOS 27.3 is also required. The features can be enabled in the Watch app on the iPhone.


Apple Intelligence for China

‌Apple Intelligence‌ is now live in China. It includes initial ‌Apple Intelligence‌ features like Live Translation, Writing Tools, Visual Intelligence, email and notification summaries, ‌Photos‌ Clean Up, and Genmoji.



‌Siri‌ AI is not available, nor are the ‌Apple Intelligence‌ features added in ‌iOS 27‌.

China Earthquake Alerts

iOS 27.3 appears to add support for safety alerts. Apple has been working with the China Earthquake Networks Center to add early warning earthquake alerts for users in China.

Selfie Sing

Apple Music has a new "Selfie Sing" option that lets users capture a video of themselves singing karaoke. The feature can be found by searching for the ‌Apple Music‌ Sing playlist in ‌Apple Music‌, selecting a song, and then tapping on the camera icon to start a recording. 



Karaoke videos can be adjusted wit voice modification options and shared with friends or on social media.

Freeform

In the Freeform app, there are new tools for generating custom shapes and adding images. Apple says users can create custom, editable shapes with text descriptions. It's a feature limited to Apple Creator Studio subscribers.

There are also new styles for formatting text, and an option to choose a color for the background of a board.

Control Center

The VPN toggle in Control Center now lets you quickly switch between VPNs. Before now, the toggle just turned the last used VPN on or off.

App Library

The "Cancel" button in the App Library search interface is now an X button.

Apple Fitness+

iOS 27.3 includes a new Gym Strength workout in Apple Fitness+. Gym Strength is a custom fitness option that generates a four-week plan based on a user's goals, experience, schedule, and equipment.



Safari Settings

In the Advanced section of Safari settings, there's an option to "Use Global Privacy Control."



Weather

The tiny slider that lets you swap between Condition views in the Weather app now uses Liquid Glass. Apple has also updated how next-hour precipitation looks. 


Australia

RCS support is available for Australian carrier Telstra in iOS 27.3.

title: Apple Music's New Selfie Sing Feature Lets You Record Karaoke Videos
content:
iOS 27.3 adds a new "Selfie Sing" feature in Apple Music that lets users record themselves while singing a song.


There's a dedicated Selfie Sing playlist and a selfie camera view that shows lyrics on the screen while also recording a video. Apple has a description of the feature:
There are some songs everyone knows by heart, the ones that come on and suddenly the whole room's singing along. This playlist is loaded with them, each one ready to become your next Selfie Sing. Pick your favorite, record a Selfie Sing, add mic effects to your voice, then save or share your video selfie with anyone you like. No pitch-perfect anything required–just you, the song, and the moment. Oh, and make sure you've updated to the latest iOS before getting started.

After selecting a song, you can tap on the camera icon to start a Selfie Sing. Tapping the red button begins a recording, and the lyrics start to scroll by. When a song is finished, there are options to change the volume of your voice or add an effect. Options include Megaphone, Echo, Concert Hall, and Studio. Videos can then be saved to the Photos library or shared.


Here is your first look at Selfie Sing, new in iOS 27.3, inside of Apple Music

Record a video selfie, adjusting vocals to make it yours, and share your performance with friends

— Aaron (@aaronp613) November 4, 2026



Songs on the Selfie Sing playlist include "Respect" by Aretha Franklin, "Girls Just Wanna Have Fun" by Cyndi Lauper, "Like a Virgin" by Madonna, "Wonderwall" by Oasis, "Hungry Like the Wolf" by Duran Duran, and "Baby One More Time" by Britney Spears.

There isn't an option to take a Selfie Sing recording on every ‌Apple Music‌ song, but that could be something coming in the future. Selfie Sing appears to be an extension of the ‌Apple Music‌ Sing karaoke feature that came out in iOS 16.2.

title: Apple officially restricts employee participation in prediction markets
content:
If you're an Apple employee or contractor planning to make money using insider information to gamble in legally-gray "prediction markets," don't. Apple has made its stance clear in a new filing.


Don't bother using insider information to gamble in prediction markets
Prediction markets skirt the legal definition of gambling, which means they have become widely available in the United States in spite of gambling laws. These markets can be used to bet on everything from when a location might see its first snow to what colors the latest iPhones will be sold in.
Regardless of the legality of these markets, Apple has made it clear that using insider information to participate is considered insider trading. While the companies like Polymarket already have insider trading rules, these enable Apple to act against violators from their end.

title: iPhone Jailbreak Gets Past Lockdown Mode and Survives an Update
content:

Calif shared a video of a jailbroken iPhone 18 Pro with Lockdown Mode on. From there, iOS 27.2 is installed, and the jailbreak remains in place after the update. It isn't clear whether the jailbreak could be installed on a device already running iOS 27.2.

FaceTime calls from unfamiliar callers, disabling invites for Apple services, and removing location information from photos.


Lockdown Mode helps, until it doesn't. https://t.co/1UyxPHQUAe
— Calif (@calif_io) November 3, 2026



The video shows a malicious PDF sent to the target iPhone using AirDrop to initiate the jailbreak, with the file accepted by the user. Calif hasn't shared additional information, and the exact jailbreak steps are unknown. 

Apple told TechCrunch that it was not aware of any successful mercenary spyware attacks against an iPhone in Lockdown Mode.

title: Apple Watch Activity badges: Veteran’s Day challenge on November 11
content:
Macworld





Achievement badges are a funny thing. You know they’re just a simple little bit of visual flair, they don’t even do anything, and yet for some reason you just have to collect them. Gamification can be a great motivator, and the achievement badges for the activity tracking on the Apple Watch have inspired many users to get more exercise. 
If you want to maximize your badge count, you’re going to want to chase down as many activity achievements as you can. Most are available year-round, but there are also some time-limited special events to grab, too. Here’s a list of all the activity achievements for the Apple Watch and how to unlock them. 
Updated November 3, 2026: Apple’s yearly Veteran’s Day challenge is coming up on November 11, 2026.
Apple Watch Series 12 (42mm)
